maintopic: EXTENSION OF RESTRICTIONS TO ADDITIONAL CLASSES OF CONSTRUCTION

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: EXTENSION OF RESTRICTIONS TO ADDITIONAL CLASSES OF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
I wish to make a brief statement on the supply situation affecting steel.
In my remarks in the house last Thursday I indicated that further orders might be necessary to protect supplies of steel for essential construction projects. Order No. 3 was issued on Friday last. This order restricts the use of steel for a wide range of construction projects. Order No. 1, which was issued last December, remains in effect until March 1, when order No. 3 becomes effective in its place.
This extension of restrictions to additional classes of construction has been made necessary by the increasing requirements of steel for urgent projects which are essential to our
252	HOUSE OF
Restrictions on use of steel preparedness program. For instance, we must assure adequate supplies of steel for construction of radar stations, military barracks and other pi ejects which are required for the armed services. Also, we must assure a supply of steel for the construction of factories for the immediate production of aircraft, radar equipment and other military items. Equally important for the long pull to our joint defence efforts with other members of the United Nations is the expansion of Canadian capacity to produce strategic raw materials and to provide transportation and other essential services for the defence program. It has become apparent during recent weeks that in order to proceed with these urgent defence projects, restrictions must be placed on less essential types of construction.
My order No. 1 restricted use of steel for a few classes of construction, such as places of amusement, entertainment or recreation; construction for the merchandising, storage, manufacturing or processing of liquors, spirits, beers or wines; construction for the manufacturing or processing of tobaccos, cigarettes, cigars, carbonated beverages or confectionery; as well as use of steel for outdoor advertising signs. Order No. 3 adds to this list a wide range of other construction, including office buildings, hotels, printing establishments, banks, construction for the purpose of furnishing personal services, construction for the purpose of storing, distributing or displaying consumer goods, and construction of storage warehousing for personal effects.
The administration of this order has been delegated to the recently-established steel division of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Because of the critical supply situation for steel for construction projects, it will not be our policy to authorize projects on the restricted list where actual construction has not yet begun. In those cases where actual construction has begun and is well under way, it may be possible to authorize completion of the jobs, but each case will have to be considered on its own merits. It should be noted particularly that even where permission is given to complete a project on the prohibited list, this authorization does not assure availability of steel for the job, and it does not constitute any priority whatsoever for supply of the steel. It is most important that there be no confusion on this point.
Another point that probably requires some clarification is that order No. 3 restricts the use of steel materials for construction of a building. It does not restrict the use of steel for the manufacture of products such


as builders' hardware, doors, fixtures and mechanical equipment, even though such manufactured products may be incorporated in or installed in prohibited buildings. I understand that there has been a certain amount of misunderstanding on this point in connection with my order No. 1. The definitions in order No. 3 are intended to clarify this situation.
As I reported to the house last Thursday, a preliminary survey of investment intentions would indicate that private industry and government are aiming at a capital investment program in 1951 of $4,260 million, or thirteen per cent greater than in 1950. I might add that large projects are being announced almost every day, which will add to those figures. In my remarks I pointed out that it was unlikely that this objective could be attained, and that it would be necessary to restrict the use of steel and other strategic materials so that at least the more essential projects can be completed. Although order No. 3 certainly will help to assure supplies of steel for essential construction, it will not do the whole job. Further restrictions may be necessary, and I want to repeat my warning that those who contemplate construction projects, which do not relate closely to our defence effort but which are not yet on a prohibited list, should not commit themselves to building operations unless they know that they will be able to obtain the steel and other building materials needed to finish the project. It would be most unfortunate and a waste of valuable labour and materials for projects to be started and then have to be abandoned for lack of some vital material.
Because of the urgency of getting under way and completing projects that are essential to our defence preparedness program, it will be necessary to divert increasing amounts of steel and steel fabricating facilities to these top defence projects. We hope to accomplish this with a minimum disruption to less essential construction that is already under way, but it is unlikely that we can avoid altogether some hardships to those who badly need structures of the kind named in the prohibited list.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

maintopic: EMBARGO ON EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES
speechtext: Has Canada placed an embargo on the export of hides and skins from this country to the United States, and if so, why?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: EMBARGO ON EXPORTS TO UNITED STATES
speechtext:
A temporary embargo has
been established. The officials concerned with price control in the United States have placed a temporary hold on the distribution of hides and skins in that country. When the hold order was announced, buyers from the United States came to Canada and not only bought all the hides offered in our market oyer a period of time, but paid a price very much above the United States ceiling price for those hides. It was felt, and it was agreed in Washington, that a temporary embargo by Canada that would protect the action taken in the United States would be in the interests of all concerned. It will at the same time protect the supplies of leather for boots and shoes that are being ordered in great quantity for the Canadian servicemen.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, February 9, consideration of the motion of Mr. W. H. McMillan for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Drew, and the amendment to the amendment of Mr. Herridge.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday I was discussing one of the phases of the negligence of this government, having to do with immigration. I believe that this government's lack of an immigration policy is responsible for a great number of the shortages existing in this country today. Knowing the type and calibre of the persons who have come to Canada in the past, and their contribution towards the building of this country, I feel confident-as a matter of fact I am positive-that if this government had done a real job on immigration during the past five years we could have had a million willing and competent workers today for the farms and for all classes of industry. We need these people. Particularly do we need British immigrants, people who speak our language. There is no difficulty in telling a man from any part of the British isles the manner in which a certain job is to be done, especially if he is a trained artisan.
It costs the taxpayers of this country about $5,000 to educate a man or a woman. If we bring to this country people who have been educated by the European or British governments, we relieve our taxpayers of this burden, and, in most cases, receive the benefit of the presence among us of a competent person who contributes his share towards the building of this country. The people of Ontario remember with pride and admiration what was done in this regard by the then premier of the province, now the leader of the opposition in this house, when he brought to Canada ten thousand British immigrants. In checking the records showing the amounts of money which these people brought with them, I found that it totalled about $27 million. Under this plan, ten thousand British immigrants paid their way. The plan was formulated almost against the opposition of this government's department of immigration. As I have said, these people have contributed $27 million to the coffers of the Dominion of Canada.


Fortunately for the farmers of Ontario, again owing to the efforts of the present leader of the opposition, ten thousand Dutch farmers were brought to the province of Ontario. They have proven to be a godsend in the production of foodstuffs for Canada and the rest of the world. The department of immigration should be the focal point upon which this government concentrates its efforts. This government should put forth a superhuman effort in order to assure the people of Canada that this department will function as it should function, and put Canada, with its tremendous resources and its vast territory, in a position to fill the crying need for labour of the right calibre.
I shall turn now to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). It is interesting to note that on June 12, 1942, this statement was made by the hon. gentleman who is now Minister of National Defence, as reported at page 3312 of Hansard:
If, on the other hand, Canada fails by even a hairbreadth to discharge her full duty to the united nations, to humanity and to herself, she would be dishonoured . . .
This statement should be recalled when we look at the position in which the people of Canada find themselves today. In this morning's newspapers we read that that famous and gallant regiment, the Princess Patricia's light infantry, is about to enter the front line in Korea. Here is history repeating itself, just as surely as we are sitting in this House of Commons. If these men, who volunteered to uphold the honour of Canada, run into any fighting, it will be history repeating itself; they will be short of reinforcements from Canada. To realize the truth of this, one needs only to reflect on the first real battle in which the Canadian army engaged at Ypres in 1915, when approximately fifteen thousand fighting men were wiped out in about twenty-four hours.
There are no strings attached to soldiers in the fighting line. You cannot tell them to go forward and then pull them back by the strings if they are surrounded by the enemy. How dearly we would have loved to be able to pull back these men at Ypres, who were surrounded by the enemy because of the breaking of certain of our allies on our left. The Germans surrounded the Canadians and marched them oil by companies:, that is, those who survived the unseen gas attack. If these gallant men of the Princess Patricia's light infantry are the victims of such a slaughter, where are the reinforcements for them? The Conservative government of 1914-18 was lax in securing adequate reinforcements. Men had to serve two terms'

in the front-line trenches, in water up to their knees. We who served in that war said that if there were ever another war we would see to it that these conditions were not repeated.
What did we find in 1939? We found-and you know it is true, for the facts were divulged by a gallant member of this House of Commons, Colonel Ralston-that there were no reinforcements for our men. This hon. member resigned from the ministry as a protest to the Liberal government against the lack of reinforcements for the fighting men in Italy. He knew the facts, because he had visited the scene. History did repeat itself. The same dilatory methods as those used by the Conservative government in 1914-18 were continued by this government. But this government had the example of the results of lack of reinforcements, and paid no attention to it. This government had the example of the heartfelt calls of the fighting soldiers for more reinforcements, for a bit of needed rest, during the war of 1939-45. So far their cries and their demands for preparation have been allowed to go unheeded. One does not need to be a military expert to realize what will happen in Korea if our poor soldiers do their part, as they will, and fight as all Canadian soldiers have always fought, with no thought of retreat when surrounded. They will carry on the traditions of Canadian fighting men. When what may be the remnants reassemble back of the line, and they are asked to go up into the fighting line again without adequate support, what will they think? They will think as we thought in the war of 1914-18, and as the boys thought in the war of 1939-45: "I suppose our parliament is doing the right thing." You and I know that this parliament did not do the right thing. The Tory parliament did not do the right thing. But let it not be said of this government that it did not do the right thing.
The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) stated in this house last week that we were proud of the efforts of Canadian soldiers in the last two wars. That is true. But we are not proud of the reinforcement effort put forward by either the Conservative government or the Liberal government in the past two wars. Our armies made history for themselves, and our factory workers made history for themselves, but with little semblance of guidance or encouragement by the present government.
We can easily remember the request which came from the British government for the opportunity to train British pilots in this country; and we can recall, with not a great deal of pride, the response that came to that
The Address-Mr. Ferguson request, and how late-but fortunately not too late-it was acceded to. We recall that those marvellous boys from the British isles came out to Canada and trained, returned to the British isles and flew aircraft in all parts of the world in order to crush the curse of Hitlerism. Let that situation not occur again. Every member of this House of Commons has a duty to perform, even those on the Liberal benches; and it is a duty that the people sent them here to perform. Irrespective of politics I suggest that hon. members go to their cabinet ministers and say: Please let us not have a repetition of the past. We are at war. Our men are going into battle today. We are stiff allowing certain factories to make non-essentials. We are still permitting a communist rally in Massey hall in Toronto, in spite of the fact that communist soldiers in Korea are murdering wounded men. We need no proof of that. We know the type and calibre of men we are dealing with so far as our enemy is concerned.
We are gradually pushing our men into the front line. Are we in Canada prepared for this situation? Do you feel in your hearts that it is the right thing to do to have these men in battle and at the same time to permit Tim Buck to eulogize the communists and their fellow-travellers, for them to cheer the remarks made by that man and for him to delude the minds of Canadians by the thousands when we are at war?
The backseat generals in the Dominion of Canada have been prone to criticize a great man, General MacArthur, who is carrying out a job with men who are not trained sufficiently to enter battle. He is carrying out a job against as ruthless an enemy as the world has ever known. General MacArthur should receive praise from the lips of every person this side of the iron curtain for the great show of generalship he has made on behalf of all the nations and peoples of the United Nations. General Eisenhower, a man of whom we are very proud, has now taken over the organizing of the defence of Europe. This city of Ottawa had the honour of having this great man visit it. I hope that when he delivered his secret messages to the cabinet, he impressed on their minds the seriousness of the situation in the world today, with the threat of the communist hordes. If they will only act as men capable of filling the positions they occupy, his visit was well worth while. The people of Canada are waiting patiently to see immediate steps taken, with no further procrastination, with respect to things that have to be done, that should be done, and that can be done. In my opinion this government will go down in history and be known
256	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Sinclair as the "dio-nothing Liberal government". It is about the worst of its kind that we have ever known in Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first words in this debate must be words of congratulation to both the mover (Mr. McMillan) and the seconder (Mr. Breton) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. As they were speaking I felt very close to them. One reason was a physical one, in that I sat between them; and in the second place, eleven years ago I had the same pleasant task myself. I was not surprised at the excellence of the quality of their speeches, because men who could come here, one with as big a majority as that of the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan), and the other by that most wonderful of all political accomplishments, a political acclamation, are obviously men who are held in high repute in their constituencies. What I admired about them, sitting as close to them as I do, was the coolness and calmness with which they presented their maiden messages to this house. I think they will have fine careers in this chamber.
No doubt one of the reasons why they were able to acquit themselves so well when for the first time they spoke in parliament in the presence of these veterans of so many political battles was the advice they had undoubtedly received from the more senior members in their areas. I myself can remember getting excellent advice when I was chosen for this task and sought the counsel of one who was then the senior member from British Columbia; I refer to the late Ian Mackenzie. He gave me excellent advice, although I did not follow it as well as I should have. Had I done so, my maiden speech might have been more successful. In any case he concluded by saying, "Jimmie, there will be another thing you will need for your speeches. You will need a small trunk and a big trunk". I said, "What for?" He said, "A small trunk in which to keep the speeches you actually make in the House of Commons, and a big trunk in which to put all the speeches that you prepared for delivery but which for one reason or another you did not make." Well,
I didn't get those trunks; but if I had them today perhaps I should put the speech which I am now about to make in the bigger trunk, because it was prepared for an occasion which has not developed. I try to be a good parliamentary assistant, to earn the pay about which the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) talks so much, by following very closely in the House of Commons the speeches and activities of hon. members relating to our own Department of Finance. I also follow the speeches they make outside the house. There are some members who are as


quiet as field mice when they are in the House of Commons surrounded by their equals, but when they get back in the bosom of their own ridings and with their political associates, they roar like lions. There are other members, however, who are vigorous in the House of Commons and equally vigorous outside the House of Commons. I watch their speeches outside with especial interest, because what they say just before a session is probably what they are going to say during the session.
It was with this attitude that I read with great surprise a Canadian Press account of a speech made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), who I am sorry to say is now absent. I sent him a note just a moment ago telling him that I was going to devote some time to him, and hoped he would stay. Perhaps I shall be forgiven if I seem to be attacking him in his absence. Probably he will come back.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He will be back.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
In a Canadian Press account of October 25 from Saskatoon, the following appears:
Saskatoon, October 25 (CP)-George Drew, national leader of the Progressive Conservative party, said Tuesday night that the government can save $500 million a year by eliminating wasted spending. It would help combat the growing dangers of inflation.
Mr. Drew said in an address that savings proportionate to those outlined for the United States government by the Hoover commission could be made by Ottawa. This could be accomplished without interfering with necessary services and defence expenditures.
Well, my first reaction to that was, this must be a typographical error. It appeared in the Vancouver Sun. I looked up some other papers to see if I could see this Canadian Press account. I looked up the Saskatchewan papers. Sure enough, it was not $5 million; it was not $50 million; it was $500 million- half a billion dollars.
My second reaction was: how unfair to parliament! We have heard those speeches by many of the Conservative members, especially addressed to my minister, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott). We have heard expressions about contempt of parliament when he at one time had to go on the radio between sessions and tell, not his party followers but all the people of Canada, about the changes in taxation which would have to be effected.
The leader of the opposition is also paid a salary. He too has responsibilities to parliament, and surely if in that silver-thatched head of his he has knowledge of how to save half a billion dollars a year it should have been given to parliament during the last

session. It should have been given to the public accounts committee during the last session. It should not be given only to a group of his party followers out in Saskatoon, after the session is over.
My third reaction was: how unfair to the people of Canada; because, as he says, one of the best ways to combat inflation today is to curb all unnecessary government spending. The people of Canada are the ones who have suffered most if he could, as he said, have pruned $500 million from this year's estimates.
My fourth reaction was a personal one. How unfair it was to the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), the financial critic of the Tory party. On occasion during budget debates I may have been a little hard on the hon. member. I know the difficult position he is in. The minister presents his budget, and a week later the hon. member replies. In the interval between, the people of Canada have shown acceptance of the budget, and he has then the very difficult task of criticizing. If the leader of the opposition had only told his trusted colleague how he could make this $500 million saving, what a speech he could then have made last session! He could have told the Minister of Finance not just how to raise the $50 million deficit, but how to acquire a surplus of $450 million as well. Well, I was sure that one question the leader of the opposition would raise immediately parliament opened was this tremendously important domestic issue, the saving of $500 million on our present estimates. Therefore I decided to do some work. I have done quite a bit of work on it, much more work than is indicated in the documents I have in my hand.
If I had any doubts whether or not I should work on this, those doubts were certainly resolved by a very strong editorial in a great Conservative paper in my home town in British Columbia, the Vancouver Daily Province, of October 27, which reads as follows:
Mr. Drew makes a serious charge.
Mr. George Drew, leader of the Progressive Conservative party, speaking to a group of young workers of his party at Saskatoon this week, gave it as his opinion that the federal government could save $500 million a year by eliminating waste spending.
If Mr. Drew was speaking soberly and responsibly, he will have some grounds for his charge that half a billion dollars a year is being wasted in Canada. He will be able to go into detail-to give chapter and verse. And the people of Canada, who have a practical interest in federal expenditures, because it affects their personal spending, will listen to the indictment and demand an answer.
The charge that the Canadian government is wasting $500 million a year is a very serious charge 80709-17
The Address-Mr. Sinclair indeed: for, besides being a charge of gross extravagance, it is a charge of incompetence in administration. Half a billion dollars is one-fffth of the Canadian budget. It is twenty cents on every dollar collected in taxes from the Canadian people, who though they are prosperous enough at the moment, have no such sums to waste.
Extravagance in government is bad enough at any time, but at a time when prices are going up and dollars are going down in value, it is doubly serious. It accentuates the inflationary tendency. Since the war, the fund of purchasing power available in Canada has increased out of all proportion to the volume of goods available for purchase.
That is the stuff that makes for inflation. That is what sends prices up. And here, if Mr. Drew is correct, is an extra, irresponsible fund cf half a billion dollars, flying about uncontrolled like a loose cask on a ship's deck in a storm, and doing damage wherever it strikes. Unquestionably, something should be done about Mr. Drew's charge. Mr. Drew should see that something is done.
Well, I sat here during this debate on the motion for an address in reply to the speech from the throne. I heard the leader of the opposition speak very carefully. He actually read his speech at great length, but there was no mention at any time of this half a billion dollars. I thought perhaps I should put this speech in the big trunk, but then I thought, after all, because of the work he has put me to, I should at least give to the members of the House of Commons a synopsis of my work on this matter of government spending.
It is true that I have access to a lot of information through the Department of Finance, but I am not going to use it. I am going to use the documents which are available to any member of parliament, the estimates of Canada for this year. Let us look at these. First of all, what is the budget? The main estimates were $2,309 million, Adding the supplementary estimates we get the gross bill of $2,389,106,000. It is on these amounts that economies and savings must be effected.
The leader of the opposition was the premier of a province, so he knows that all of the formal budget is not at the disposal of any government to slash. Well, if he will say, or if one of his colleagues will say, that they want this $307 million a year, which represents a redistribution of wealth to the children of the nation, cut out, then let them say so. Otherwise I will include it.

It is actually a transfer payment of $103 million to the provinces. Through this amount we pay our three-quarters share of old age pensions. The only criticism we have heard from any quarter of the house has been that it is too low, not that it is too high, so I include it.
Then we come to the post office-and I am sorry the hon. member is not here, because the post office department was the one department for which he had a good word. On

The Address-Mr. Sinclair August 30, 1950, as reported at page 27 of Hansard, he gave his thorough approval. So I believe we can include all this, with the exception of $1,750 which he thought was too much for the little posters he showed us at the last session, urging business in Canada to make better use of the mails to get their advertising program over. If there is one organization in Canada that should certainly use this service to get their program over it is the Conservative party. The amount for the post office department is $85,663,000.
Then we come to the Department of Resources and Development. The one statutory payment here is $20 million, for the trans-Canada highway. There were many Conservative members, of course, including the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), who think it is not sufficient. No one has thought that too large.
Then we come to the R.C.M.P., and again I will take only the one statutory item, an amount of $1,188,000 for retirement pensions. We all think, I believe, that the pensions of the R.C.M.P. should not be lessened-unless of course, the Tories want to cut the scale of pensions. Unless they do, I will leave it at that.
In all the great Department of Trade and Commerce I will take just the one statutory item, dealing with coal subsidies and coal freight assistance, totalling $4,850,000. Will the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black), the hon. member from Annapolis or any other Conservative member from any of the maritime provinces, perhaps the member for Royal, say that this is a waste of money? If he will, then I will cut it off from my figures.
For all the Department of Transport I will take just the statutory payment under the Maritime Freight Rates Act totalling $7,319,000. Does any maritimer want this cut out? And we find $500,000 in that department for the railway grade crossing fund. We spend that each year, and in view of the grade crossing fatalities, we should be spending more. And unless the hon. member for York West (Mr. Adamson) who has spoken so much on it wants to have it cut down, we will leave it as it is. Finally there is the Department of Veterans Affairs. If there is one thing we have heard in this house again and again and again, it is the Tory criticism that we are spending too little on every aspect of veterans affairs, that we have not been generous enough. Since they want no economies here I will include the $198,881,000. Now all these statutory payments and the things that the Tory party has said are sound, and on some of which we are criticized for not spending enough, add up in the main estimates to
[Mr. Sinclair.l

$1,734,655,000. Mind you, we have the supple-mentaries, and I added their total to the figure of gross expenditure I gave for the main estimates. Picking out in these sup-plementals the statutory items, and adding the cost of the Manitoba flood and the Rimouski and Cabano fires-and I do not think the Tories said that was wasteful-we find another $21,161,000 of statutory payments in the supplementals. Therefore this brings the whole area of controlled expenditure, controlled by statute, controlled by thorough approval of the Tory party, up to the sum of $1,745,816,000. If we subtract that from the gross of our main estimates and our sup-plementaries, the figure of $2,389,000,000 to which I referred, we get left $643,290,000 as the area for all government departments in which there are controllable expenditures of every sort, and on that the leader of the opposition says he can save $500 million-not 20 per cent but 80 per cent economies on all the many activities of government in the federal field.
Of course hon. members know how he is going to justify it. "Hoover commission" are going to be the great words. If we could only make a saving similar to the Hoover commission, he will say, all would be well. I have done quite a bit of work on the Hoover commission. I would not have done so unless the hon. member had made that speech, but I am glad I did. I learned a lot. First of all, is it a good basis of comparison to compare our type of government, our cost of government, with that of the United States? Very few political economists of repute have ever thought that was true. One of the great works is that of the late Lord Bryce, "Modern Democracy." It is an excellent analysis of the differences between England, the United States and ourselves.
The United Kingdom is a small, compact country with a well-established government, most of the public facilities long since built up and paid for, a unitary form of government, just one level and then the borough down below, and parliamentary control over expenditures. It is a naturally efficient way, an excellent way of government. As for ourselves, we are a comparatively new government on the federal system. We have a comparatively small population, spread over an enormous territory, which naturally makes for expense in administration; an expanding economy demanding every day new and better public facilities to serve our expanded agriculture and expanded industry. We have a good civil service. We are getting away as fast as we can from the old evils of political patronage. There are few political appointments today.

speechtext: Since when?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Then we can point to the fact that we have the British parliamentary system of control, the treasury board, the Auditor General, the comptroller general, the committee of the whole house, and the public accounts committee if the opposition will make it work. In a system like ours there may be however more opportunity for overlapping than in the United Kingdom, and for more costly administration.
But when, we turn to the United States we find a very large population in a large country. That in itself makes it tremendously difficult to have a compact efficient administration. It also is a federal and not a unitary system. There is separation of the legislative body from the executive, both with powers of political appointment, a weak civil service compared with ours or the British, no auditor general, and no government responsibility for initiating money legislation. Any congressman, any senator or the executive branch can initiate such money legislation. They take their politics much more seriously in a political way. There is a great change in ordinary civil service positions when there is a change of the party in power as the result of an election, all adding to the cost of government.
Finally-and I believe this was mentioned long ago by Lord Bryce-there is the American Tammany hall maxim, a maxim which is used a great deal, and which perhaps still influences United States politics too much, that for successful re-election you must never vote for a tax bill and you must never oppose a public expenditure. When you make that comparison, you will of course see that there will be more need for savings by improving the administration under the United States system than under our system, and probably more need under our system than under the British system. However, let us go ahead with the comparison despite the difference in position.
I have done a lot of work on the Hoover commission, and so far the most optimistic report I have been able to find is that published by the civil service assembly, the group most strongly in favour of the Hoover commission in volume 17, No. 1 of their journal for January, 1951. It points out that, counting everything they possibly can, taking credit for all savings, they have effected savings of $2 billion in a budget of roughly $40 billion, or five per cent. Our budget of course is $2,500 million, and if our economy were the same, which it is not, if our government were the same, the savings would be $125 million, not the $500 million of the leader of the opposition.
The Address-Mr. Sinclair
More than that, the government rate of spending in the United States is very much greater than ours. Last year they spent $266 a person, and we spent $164 a person. The leader of the opposition will say more will be saved when all the commission report is implemented. I find that this blind faith in commissions, which the leader of the opposition has so far as the Hoover commission is concerned, is not shared by all people. For example, I remember that he himself started the Hope commission three years ago when he was premier of Ontario. When the Hope commission brought down its report a little while ago Premier Frost, the Conservative premier of Ontario, had this to say on February 7:
We are in no way bound to accept the recommendations of the commission.
The Conservative Ottawa Journal said in an editorial on February 9:
Premier Frost is very wise in not adopting the major recommendations of the Hope commission. He is in no way bound to accept the commission's proposals. Royal commissions are set up to report and recommend, not to make laws.
If Democratic President Truman is going to pay no more attention to the report of Republican ex-President Hoover, than Conservative Premier Frost pays to Conservative Premier Drew's royal commission, I do not think the hon. leader of the opposition can expect much more in the way of economies.
I want to finish my comment on what the leader of the opposition has said with a challenge only to him. I challenge him to come into the house, to come into the public accounts committee, and, not speaking widely about the Hoover commission, not speaking vaguely of percentages but as the Province editorial said, chapter and verse, item by item, say what services can be dispensed with and what employees can be dismissed. Then I will total his figures, and I shall be pleased if he can make this saving of $500 million out of the $667 million which is controllable. The people of Canada will be pleased. The government will be pleased.
There is one other thing I should like to say about him before I leave him. I should like to give him a little advice. He is not here, but he will read it in Hansard. He would not take it anyway from me.

speechtext: Who would?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
There is a wonderful series of essays by Thomas Carlyle on hero worship. Naturally the leader of the opposition's followers try to pattern their conduct on their leader, just as I probably try to pattern my conduct on that of the Minister of Finance, a good model, though I am not very successful. There is one young member in

The Address-Mr. Sinclair particular in the opposition who is patterning himself very closely on his leader, the young and gallant member for Broadview (Mr. Hees). The leader of the opposition has the responsibility of making sure that the pattern this young member is following is a good one. I do not think it is such a good one right now, and we see evidence of that in the house.
As I pointed out, the leader of the opposition is careless with figures. His young follower, who came immediately after him in the debate, is also careless with figures. I say he is careless because in his speech, to be found at page 61 of Hansard, he compared our armed forces with those of Great Britain, and said that the armed forces of Great Britain totalled 1,023,000 men. Of course he may have authority, but I should like to refer to another authority, Prime Minister Attlee, speaking in the British House of Commons on January 29. His remarks are to be found in Canadian newspapers of that date, and in the airmail edition of the London Times which was available in the reading room on the 30th. Prime Minister Attlee said that in the last white paper strength of the armed forces, men in uniform, was 682,000 but that by April they hoped, by calling up many more reserves and extending compulsory training, to get it up to 800,000. The hon. member for Broadview is still not quite as reckless as his leader, but he is inclining that way when 800,000 next April is quoted as 1,023,000 today.
The second point is this matter of being careless in the basis of comparison. The leader of the opposition compares Canada with the United States. He says that our governments are the same, and the overlapping and inefficiency are the same. I say that is wrong. His young follower then compares Great Britain's manpower problem and our manpower problem and gives that as a reason why we are failing to put enough men in the army.
There are great differences on any basis, but let us look at Britain as far as manpower is concerned. They cannot feed themselves. The fifty thousand farmers who would be required to grow wheat in Britain, if they could grow wheat there, can be put in the army. We feed ourselves, and in addition we have to take fifty thousand men out of the manpower pool and put them on the prairies to grow wheat for Britain, plus all the men needed to service these farms and transport the wheat. Then we have seventeen thousand men up in Sudbury in nickel production, much of which goes to Britain. That takes men from our supply which Britain
(Mr. Sinclair.]

does not have to do. Ten per cent of our working force in British Columbia is employed producing timber for Britain today. The same thing is true of our base metals, oil, newsprint. These are things they cannot do for themselves, and of course that is why our scale of participation must be different from that of Britain. Of all the North Atlantic countries, Canada and the United States have the greatest resources; and in this cold war that is going on at the present time the production of equipment and the development of resources to get ready to defend ourselves are the overriding factors. We must divide our manpower between our resources and our armed forces for the best advantage of all our allies.
My hon. friend's leader skirted all around this manpower issue, both the conscription and compulsory service issue, as was pointed out by the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank). So did the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) and the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes). Out on the west coast we heard different statements by all three Conservative members, trying to kid the Canadian Legion into believing that they were endorsing their program. Although there is not much need for me to do so, I believe this would be a good time to place my views on record in this respect. Hon. members will remember that last fall the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) very kindly and thoughtfully quoted from one of my old speeches, made in 1944, in which I gave my stand on conscription. I said I still believed every word of it, but of course he did not commit himself at that time. I was proud of the brave, straightforward statement the Prime Minister made at the start of the debate on manpower. I was ashamed of the scuttling and scurrying of the Conservative party on the same issue.
I believe with the Prime Minister the use of manpower for the development of our resources and industry to help build up the North Atlantic defences is the overriding need today; but I also believe, and I have told the Prime Minister, that while we may not, because of labour shortages, be able to drain off our eighteen and nineteen-year-olds for two years of compulsory service as do other countries, we can begin such training without losing manpower from industry. First compulsory service in the cadet corps of our high schools. I had that training, and I am sure it did me no great harm. Those going to our universities are indirectly in receipt of state assistance for at least half their tuition and they also should be asked to take compulsory training as their contribution in return. Then our young men who are all working today in industry, and who

should stay working, and who spend their evenings at hockey games or basketball matches, at the movies, at dances and in pool halls, should be called on for their duty and take time out from those activities and spend two or three nights a week during the winter and week ends during the summer training with the reserves, thus getting some training but not at the expense of our manpower requirements for industry.
I see my time is almost up; I have only six minutes left, and I still have a great deal of material. In these six minutes I will not have time to cover everything I had prepared, but I would like to suggest what members of parliament can do to help keep down the cost of government, because that is a tremendously important thing just now. I challenge the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew); I do not challenge any other hon. member. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) asks the co-operation of every member of this house to cut down civilian expenditures in every possible way. Last year I gave the house examples when I told hon. members what the treasury board does in holding down government spending. We have all these very desirable expenditures, for public facilities and services suggested by hon. members or by communities in the country which they persuade the appropriate minister to include in his estimates. The ministers go before treasury board, and desirable though these projects may be they are not approved. Of course the Minister of Finance is the awful ogre who is blamed for stopping the member or the community from getting this very desirable service. Well, somebody has to do that job and the taxpayers of Canada should be grateful to the minister for holding the line. It is not a matter of getting rid of superfluous services in this country; there are so many desirable things which need to be done in this expanding nation but treasury board has to decide which of those things are most desirable in view of funds available.
How can members help? Well, I think the first way in which members can help is by using some restraint in their own demands upon ministers and the government for more facilities and services for their ridings. I remember last year, when the Minister of Finance placed restrictions on capital expenditures for new public buildings. Who were the first to bob up? They were the Conservative member for Queens (Mr. McLure) and the Conservative member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles)-

I will certainly put the record straight, but those were the first members to bob up. They said, "Yes, we agree, but we hope that will not affect the post offices at Charlottetown and Winnipeg." Economies always begin in the ridings of other members. I have prepared something of an analysis of what hon. members have asked of parliament; and I am sorry the hon. member for Van-couver-Quadra is not here, because he was one of the best examples of an economy-minded Conservative. I went through Hansard for 1949; the index for 1950 is not ready yet so I could not search 1950 easily. I read all the speeches of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra in 1949, and in doing that I certainly earned my pay. I should like to read this summary of my findings, but I have not time. Here are thirty items, ranging all the way from a Pacific pact to a complete trans-Canada highway system of several roads including lighthouses on the Queen Charlotte islands, $50 at sixty-five for everybody, agricultural floor prices, bigger travel bureau, Alaskan railway and so on. With the- pricing I have been able to give, on those items where he was specific enough to make a calculation in that one year the hon. member advocated projects which would require an extra expenditure of $800 million; and taking into account the many other things he advocated, such as the Pacific pact and a modern merchant marine, which are difficult to price exactly I would say conservatively-that is in the old sense, not the spendthrift Progressive-Conservative sense-he would have added $1,500 million to the budget of Canada that year if the government had adopted all his suggestions, not bad for one economy-minded Conservative. This list is quite open to any hon. member who would like to see it.
When I was reading through his speeches I was also looking for something else, for any suggestion of economies in other departments which might make funds available for his projects, and most important of all for any suggestions as to how taxes might be increased in order to pay for just one of these new projects. Nothing of the kind was mentioned anywhere. There was no mention at all of any other tax. On the contrary he and his party have always opposed every tax proposal brought in by the Minister of Finance. In this house there is no more devout believer than the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra in that old Tammany hall precept I quoted earlier: never vote for a tax measure and never oppose a public expenditure. The hon. member goes a little further and suggests plenty of new expenditures.

The Address-Mr. Fulton That is not going to cut down the cost of government-that is not going to save $500 million out of the present budget.
Members of parliament can be of great help if, instead of fishing around the estimates in the House of Commons or in the public accounts committee, they would look around their own ridings. We do have these treasury board controls all through the departments looking for internal economies; but the people who can do a better job externally are the members back in their ridings and their constituents who are even better judges of where economies can be made without impairing needed service. These savings should be made where services are superfluous. Let them come here and tell the minister: "That service in my riding is no longer needed, we can do without it; these employees are no longer necessary" and they will be making a real contribution. If in that way they can effect any economy, not necessarily of half a billion dollars but of half a million dollars, half a thousand dollars, or even half a hundred dollars, the Minister of Finance will be grateful because it will lessen his burden; the government of Canada will certainly be grateful, and the people of Canada will be most grateful of all because then we members of parliament will be doing a real job in our own field in fighting inflation.

This is a serious matter, Mr. Speaker, opening as it does a breach in this principle of cabinet solidarity. I know that parliamentary assistants are not paid as much as our cabinet ministers, and I do not begrudge them their salaries in so far as they do the work and get an insight into the workings of the government; but for my own part 1 believe that when they accept that appointment as parliamentary assistant they should then see to it that, on all matters of national policy and matters which are issues of the moment, they take care not to go off at a tangent from the government. If they do so, and if that practice is persisted in and enlarged, as it undoubtedly would be, it would mean the end of the principle of


cabinet solidarity. Having said that, perhaps we can leave the matter for the moment.
There is one other matter to which I wish to refer, and which arises out of the speech of the hon. member who has just concluded his remarks, before I turn to the subject I myself wish to discuss this afternoon. He referred to the statement of the hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Hees) and implied that he was careless with figures. I am informed by the hon. member for Broadview that the figures he used with respect to the strength of the British armed forces-and I point out that they were with respect to the armed forces, not just army-were given to him by the British information office in this city just shortly before he spoke.
The other matter was an attempt by the hon. member to suggest that the hon. member for Broadview had evaded the question of how the manpower for the armed forces should be raised. Once again I regret that the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) appears to have worked diligently but in a rather misplaced fashion; because if he had been more disposed really to study that speech in order to see if there were suggestions in it, he would have found that the hon. member for Broadview laid down a specific and clear-cut six-point program incorporating his suggestions as to how our armed forces should be raised.
This afternoon, Mr. Speaker, I want to say a word or two with respect to the program outlined so far by the government for the purpose of placing this country in a position to meet the crisis in international affairs with which we are now faced. I hope I will not be thought to be unduly critical when I say that what we have had so far are, in the main, broad generalizations-an indication of goals or objectives-but not much in the way of detail as to how we are to get them. The broad objectives are all very well and are of course an essential part of the information we must have in order to assess the merits or otherwise of the government's programs for this and succeeding years; but what I think we must concern ourselves with more than ever is the question of whether the plans are adequate even to meet the objectives which the government has laid down. In other words we must say to the government, "You have told us what you are going to do. You are going to raise so many men for national defence and spend so many billions of dollars-$5 billion in the next three years-on arming and equipping those forces. That is all very well, but now tell us how you propose to do it."
My own views with respect to the methods to be followed in the raising of our defence

forces are on the record both in and out of this house. Nothing that has occurred since has caused me in the slightest degree to modify or change those views; I still hold and advocate them as strongly as ever. But the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) has told us that the government does not propose to change its methods for the time being. While I do not in any way accept this answer as final or satisfactory, I do not propose at this moment to elaborate my own views but rather to deal with the government's program in the light of the present facts and within the limitations of the government's own policy. I believe that those facts show that the government's policy is inadequate and that its program will not work.
However, just before turning to an examination of this program, I should say that I support to the full the remarks made on Monday last by the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) to the effect that the urgency of the situation is such that the government should lose no time in putting itself in a position where other and more vigorous steps, actually in the contemplation of the Prime Minister himself, can be taken to place this country in a position of readiness. The words of the hon. member for Nanaimo were so significant and they put the whole position so clearly that I think I am justified in reading them into the record again. They are found at page 99 of Hansard of February 5 and are as follows:
It would, however, seem to me only common prudence that the government should at this time set up the machinery which may be necessary to accelerate its method of enlistment, its method of assigning the manpower of the country to the various services and to industry, agriculture, transport and all the rest of it. If these steps are left to the eleventh hour I feel that it will not be possible to take full advantage of the resources of this country, both in manpower and in materials. Therefore I feel there is no time to be lost in carrying out a review both of our assets and of our deficiencies. I feel that that review should be carried out at once so that the government will be in a position to change its present method of providing for the expansion which has been indicated, should the methods that it proposes to follow immediately fail, or should the situation deteriorate to such an extent that other methods would have to be followed. There is no time to be lost in making the preparations and in setting up the machinery so that a more vigorous system of supplying the material and the personnel for expansion can be followed, and to set up this machinery there are many requirements.
The reasons why I feel that the urgency of the situation justifies those remarks appear quite clearly from the statements of the ministers themselves. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) have both told us that the international situation was
The Address-Mr. Fulton never more serious. Then the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) followed with an outline of what this government's program is to meet that situation. You will remember that he gave us fifteen points and in general outlined a program calling for expansion of our armed forces to 115,000 men and the expenditure of $5 billion. What this house and the country should now be told is when this program is to be completed and by what means. Is the government ready with its specific proposals now as to how the men, materials and money are to be found to fulfil that program?
Nothing said so far justifies the hope that they are ready. Personally I doubt it.
I hope the ministers are ready with their detailed proposals. I hope the estimates are ready so that as soon as this debate is over, which will probably be in a short time now, we can examine the details of how the defence department proposes to raise, equip and train the men, and how the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) proposes to procure the raw materials on which so large a part of the $5 billion will be spent. Are the estimates of the defence production department ready? Is the government ready to set up that department immediately? I hope they are and I believe the people hope so too, so they will know the government is ready with action to meet this emergency and to fulfil the program which they themselves have outlined.
No one knows, Mr. Speaker, just how long we may have. We can talk about programs, but the Russians in Europe and the Chinese in Asia are calling the shots.
We may have a year or two years or three years, but we may only have as many months. What plans has the government to deal with the situation which will develop if it should turn out that we have only a month or two or three months? When he spoke on Thursday, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) certainly did not indicate that he would have any substantial part of his program in operation within six months.
I hope the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is ready with his budget and his other proposals as to how best to raise the money to make this tremendous effort. Is he ready particularly with his program and proposals as to how the present inflationary pressure is to be arrested? How does he propose to see to it that this $5 billion is pumped into our already tight-stretched economy without aggravating inflation to the extent referred to by Mr. Donald Gordon in his speech that has already been quoted in this house? This house and the country will want to know
268

The Address-Mr. Fulton what plans the minister and the government have for dealing with inflation if it should actually reach the point referred to by Mr. Gordon, when it becomes that most dreaded of all things-runaway inflation.
And incidentally, Mr. Speaker, how much further does the government feel that we have to go before that point is reached? I wonder whether the government appreciates to the full the dreadful squeeze which is being felt now by the consumers of this country-the Ordinary men and women of Canada. The people of this country are in a position where they desperately need something to be done now to help them. Prices have already gone up enormously and the trend is being aggravated by every statement that the government makes threatening further and increasing shortages of both basic materials and consumer commodities. Of course prices are bound to go up when such statements are made and so much money is pumped into the stream of competitive buying, and no steps are taken to control the pressure. This house and the country, Mr. Speaker, will want something better than the statement of the Minister of Trade and Commerce on Thursday, which when you analyse it amounted to nothing much more than a lame plea that we cannot really do anything by locking the stable door after the horse has been stolen.
And incidentally, it is very noteworthy what a different and timorous attitude the government takes this time from its attitude previously with respect to measures to control inflation. We all remember how, particularly in the post-war years, when we thought we were back again to a peacetime economy and controls were being discussed, the government used to boast about the promptitude with which it had acted in 1941 to keep costs down by its anti-inflationary program. We all remember how they used to boast-and with, I think, justifiable pride-that when the Americans came to work out a program to check inflation and rising costs there they studied carefully the Canadian machinery and adopted much of it in great detail. In other words, Canada acted first and the government boasted about it in the last war, and has always taken credit previously for its own ability -to control its own affairs with respect to rising costs in this country on that occasion. This time, however, what an unfortunate reversal of attitude! The government now says that Canada itself can do nothing to control inflation but that the whole situation here depends upon what is done south of the border, and that we must wait 
for them to do it first. This country is experiencing on every hand today the outward expression of the inward policy of do-nothing Liberalism. The Minister of Trade and Commerce confirmed this when he said on Thursday, as quoted on page 186 of Hansard:
We earnestly hope our American neighbours will succeed in attaining a reasonable measure of stability; for only if that happens can we in Canada hope to avoid serious trouble.
Mr. Speaker, this sort of attitude and this sort of policy on the part of a government which is responsible to the Canadian people is not sufficient to satisfy this house and this country, which want to know what the government proposes to do to arrest the present inflationary pressures.
What plans have the ministers and the government for dealing with this situation if we should be faced with all-out war in one, two or three months instead of years? It is the responsibility of the government to prepare for this eventuality. So far the only thing we have heard of a concrete nature is that the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) expects to be ready at the end of three years-and there are grave doubts, on the basis of past records and performance, that he-or anyone else in this government-will be ready by then. So I hope the Minister of Finance and the other departments are ready with their detailed plans, proposals and answers; because, Mr. Speaker, my firm belief is that just as soon as this debate is over parliament must get down to a thorough scrutiny of the state of this nation's preparedness and of the government's plans to prepare the nation.
In particular we will want an assurance that the goods on which it is proposed to spend this five billion dollars are or will be available within the time required. What plans has the government to gear our industrial machine to the production of those specific goods and materials? Short of this assurance and outline to this house by the responsible ministers, the proposals referred to by the Minister of National Defence on Monday must be considered as paper plans.
This is no new situation that we face. This emergency has been in the contemplation of the western democracies for three years now -and we are not ready yet. I wish I could believe that the plans and programs hinted at are more than mere words; but in the light of past performance it is difficult to believe so. Let us look at the record.
In March of 1948, to go back no further, the definite possibility of immediate war

being thrust upon us was faced. The Winnipeg Free Press reported on March 10, 1948, three years ago next month:
Washington, March 10 (BUP)-United States military authorities in Germany have given up their belief that the world is relatively safe from war for at least ten years.
Informed senate sources said Tuesday this was a gist of a report made behind closed doors Monday to the senate armed services committee. It came from James Forrestal, defence secretary.
These sources said the military authorities are not necessarily predicting war. But they feel, it was said, that recent events make it necessary to reconsider their earlier estimates. Among the military experts reportedly cited by Forrestal was Gen. Lucius Clay who as United States commander in Europe has to deal with Soviet occupation forces in Germany and Austria.
Then, Mr. Speaker, to show how serious this situation was in 1948, the report concludes with these words:
Forrestal's testimony was credited with prompting the armed services committee to call immediate hearings on the controversial universal military training bill.
We are of course entitled to assume that our government was informed of that view and of the extreme gravity of the situation at that time. At that moment our armed forces were from 35 per cent to 37 per cent below their actual authorized strength and approximately 45 per cent below even the modest ceilings then set. Yet seven days later, on March 17, 1948, the Minister of National Defence assured this house that all was well and that good progress was being made.
The government did know at that time of the seriousness of the situation because the very next day, March 18, 1948, the prime minister, the late Mr. Mackenzie King-a man not given to strong statements-apparently told the Liberal party members in caucus that "the international situation had never, even in the days of Hitler, been more critical". This was three years ago next month at a time when we had only 33,000 men in our three services. Yet today after three years and the expenditure of billions of dollars we have only 62,000. The estimate for Russia and her satellites at that time was 5,032,000 men of which 4,000,000 were Russian, estimated to be fully trained and equipped. No one knows exactly how many more the Russians have now, but everyone knows, Mr. Speaker, that the Russians have not failed to make good use of the time. And yet two and a half years after the events to which I have referred, last June when a further move in the Red campaign of aggression was made in Korea, Canada was found with no army ready to send. We had had the Atlantic pact-we had had big words-
The Address-Mr. Fulton we had spent much money on defence, but the strange and deplorable fact is that June of 1950 found us with no army ready to be sent into action in the defence of democracy. And when in September of 1950, reluctantly, the decision was taken to send some troops it was necessary to raise a special force which could not be ready as a force for a year anyway. And all three services were still far below their then authorized strength.
We are told we now have 62,000 men in the three services. It has taken us three years then to build up from 33,000 to 62,000; and now we are told that we have another three-year plan-and will then have 115,000 servicemen and 33,000 civilians, a total of 148,000 actually engaged in national defence. That, Mr. Speaker, is just one per cent of our present population: and three years to get there. And if we are still as far short then of our objective as we are now we will not have attained even that limited objective.
This house therefore will want definite answers from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) on how he proposes to raise those numbers, and what are his plans for the possibility of hostilities in one, two or three months. Because time is short. He gave some figures which should arouse the greatest interest and concern. The increase for January in the three services was 2,500 men. That was the best month we have had and I understand that the department itself will be surprised if it is maintained, particularly when the competing claims of expanding defence industries are felt. But let us hope for even an average of 2,000 per month. Our objective calls for 53,000 further men for its; realization: that will take twenty-six and a half more months at present rates.
So we will want to know: What are the minister's plans for an emergency? And even in the absence of an emergency, how does he propose to guide the men and women of this country, particularly the skilled tradesmen of whom there are great shortages in both the services and in industry right now? How does he propose to guide them in making their choice so that the rate of increase in the services will be maintained? It is a problem for which the government has as yet suggested no solution.
There are some other matters on which the country and the house will want information with respect to the defence program. It has been stated from time to time, in answer to criticism from this side of the house as to the rate of expansion of the services, that we are doing very well and that in any event we have not got the facilities either in equipment, which includes accommodation as well as

The Address-Mr. Fulton arms, or training personnel, to handle any more than are coming in now. The question which must be asked is: Whose responsibility is that? And the answer of course is that it is the government's responsibility. Then the question is: Why have they no greater facilities? It certainly cannot be because they are satisfied they have enough men. A look at the recruiting advertisements contradicts that at once.
The answer then must be that the government just failed to make provision for these facilities. This brings to mind the known fact that last year the defence estimates presented by the minister to his colleagues were cut by some two hundred million dollars before they ever reached this house, and it is equally certain that this had a very serious effect on the program of the three services. Why then did the government mutilate its own defence program? And especially why did it do so at a time when the international situation, in its own words, was never more serious?
Why was no provision made for accommodation to handle an increasing inflow of recruits? Why is it that the special brigade could not be trained in this country because there was no accommodation available, but had to be sent to Fort Lewis-in a foreign country-for its training? The answer is not that it was in order to enable them to train in co-operation with the American forces for service in Korea, because this is not the fact. Our troops there are training by themselves. The simple fact is that with the international situation as serious as it was, this government neglected altogether to make any provision to place our training facilities and accommodation in a state of readiness to meet a situation which was developing daily. The country will want to know the reason for this, will hold the government responsible for this, and will want to have facts to assure them that the lost ground is being made up and that our resources and our ability to handle a greater intake of personnel are actually being increased to a degree commensurate with the seriousness of the emergency.
Another matter on which the country will want information, and this house should have information immediately, is just what is behind the present policy which appears to be complete Americanization of Canada's armed services. I refer not so much to the adoption of American type weapons and equipment, although even here there are grave reservations-because it is by no means a foregone conclusion that American arms are superior in every detail to British type. Indeed, in a substantial number of cases the opposite can be shown. However, from the point of view of production and
	i

availability of resources there is much to be said for the standardization of equipment, but I do wish to point out here that standardization should be a two-way and not only a one-way stream, and that in those respects where the British type equipment is superior we might standardize on those types.
But what I have in mind particularly here is the now very definitely discernible trend towards Americanizing the formations and training and conditions of service of the Canadian forces. We have an example in the use by the minister of the term the other night, "air division" instead of "group," and also the American term "combat team," which might mean almost anything, as against our much more exact term "brigade group." We now see by the press that the brigade which is to go to Europe is to serve as part of the American forces and not, as might have been expected, in accordance with tradition and geography, in company with the British forces.
There would seem to be no great reason for this trend except as part of the definite although always subterranean government policy of prying Canada loose from her traditional ties with the commonwealth and empire and tying her up ever more tightly with the United States. Let me ask the minister this: Does the government really believe that the American tradition, the American organization and the American method of training are superior in every respect to our own and the British? If they do, on what examples from history and experience do they base their conclusions? If they do not, for what reason are they Americanizing the Canadian formations?

speechtext: There is no basis at all in fact for what the hon. member is saying.

speechtext:
We will have more to say about it when the estimates are being considered. At that time perhaps ithe minister can explain in more detail than he has now the trend which we see in progress.
The results of this trend toward Americanization will I believe be most disastrous to the morale and fighting efficiency of Canada's army.

Speaking of the army, the minister himself has said that the basis of Canada's expanded army for participation in any actual war is the reserve force. Mr. Speaker, I have listened for a couple of weeks to this debate, and I hesitated about taking part in it. A lot of discussion has taken place on many matters, and it was all useful. As a rule I take the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne as an opportunity to air problems and grievances close to home, but at this particular time I am going to deal with what I think are the most important and serious questions confronting the parliament of Canada and the Canadian people. I am going to deal with the questions of manpower and defence, because they are so closely related.
In December of last year I was hopeful that war was a long way off and could be prevented. I pinned my hope on what had taken place at the conference of prime ministers in Great Britain. Since the end of the last war an attempt has been made by Russia largely to divide the world into two camps, communism and capitalism, and the United States foolishly fell into the trap. We all know that the bible written by Stalin is merely the bringing up to date of Leninism, and definitely tells the Russian people, and everyone within the orbit of totalitarianism today, that war between capitalism and communism is inevitable, that it has to come, that we cannot live side by side in the same worlds that either the totalitarian system must go forward and conquer the world or the world will inevitably go back to the old capitalist, imperialist regime.
That seemed to be the trend in the United Nations. The trend there was to go headlong into that kind of war. In listening to broadcasts and reading the deliberations at the prime ministers' conference, I was pleased to note that the commonwealth countries and the Scandinavian countries were getting together. I thought that they were going to be able to exert sufficient influence in the United Nations to modify United States policy and perhaps prevent for a long time-possibly for all time-a head-on clash between Russia and the United States. I was very much disappointed in what happened, and I have revised my opinion that war is a long way off. We may have a year; we may have two
272	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Gillis years; we may not have a month. It depends on the timing of Uncle Joe. If he thinks the time is right he will strike, and they always do what you do not expect them to do.
I have revised my opinion as to whether war is a long way off because of the vote of the United Nations declaring China an aggressor. Last December I was very hopeful. Since the vote' was taken I am not so hopeful. It was played up in the press and over the air that a large percentage of the members of the United Nations voted to declare China an aggressor. However, if you look at the figures you will see that there were 44 in favour, seven against and nine abstentions. The seven who opposed the resolution were members of the Soviet bloc representing the governments of 300 million people, and India and Burma with more than 300 million people, a total of 600 million. To that must be added the population of communist China of more than 400 million people. Therefore the seven against the resolution represented more than a billion people. The forty-four countries that voted for the resolution-and it seemed such a huge majority-have not a billion people. Therefore when you analyse the vote of the United Nations declaring China an aggressor the population of the countries that voted against the resolution or abstained is larger than that of the forty-four countries that supported it. Do not forget that practically all of the billion people opposing the resolution are within the communist orbit or can be absorbed very easily.
