speechtext:
Yes, or they would not be there. That is how the vote is summed up. When you declare a country an aggressor, under the United Nations machinery you have got to do something about it. Otherwise you are just making a fool of that organization. That is what leads me to believe that we should not complacently proceed in this house or


throughout the country on the assumption that we have a year, two years or three years to prepare. I hope we have got ten years but we should take the facts as they are. As I was suggesting a moment ago, the enemies that we may have to fight are countries that do not play the game as we do. They have no ethics and no morals. There is no particular line that can be followed by the old-time generals. They hit fast; there is no declaration of war. They fight a war on the basis of winning at all costs. Manpower means nothing to them; and if war comes it will be a fast one. We do not want to go along in this house or in the country on the assumption that we have the same set-up we had in 1939-40. We have not. In 1939 we had a million people unemployed in this country from whom we could draw. We had a very small national income. We had all kinds of room for industrial expansion, and we had the manpower on which we could do a fast job; and I think we did an excellent job.
Today the situation is different. The manpower position is very tight. If you had to do a fast job today I do not know where you would get the manpower. Look at the last statistical survey on the labour force in Canada issued by the Department of Labour. You will find very few spots where you can siphon off people who may be non-essential to the economy. We have a working force of approximately five million, and they are all in industries essential if the economy is to be kept moving, or industries which would have to be converted for war purposes; and if you convert them for war purposes you are increasing your manpower problem. You may get a few from those employed in trade, such as in retail stores and that sort of thing, where some 331,000 are now employed. You may get a few from the 72,000 in finance and insurance, though they would not be very good soldiers; they are not tough enough. I am sure the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) would not want to don a uniform and slug it out again. In general services across the country you have another 451,000 employees. So looking at that statistical survey we find that we have approximately 818,000 people to draw from. How many of those are fit and how many are unfit; how many would be any good for combat service and that sort of thing, I do not know, but that is about the only force in Canada on which you could draw today.
In the meantime the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) plans a large industrial expansion. He has to expand steel, and I say that is a must; that has to be done. But if he is going to expand steel he will need a great many more people in the steel industry, and I do not know where he is going

The Address-Mr. Gillis
to get them except from the group I have mentioned. So there is a great difference between our manpower problem in Canada today and the problem in 1939-40; and we must start doing some serious thinking about it.
On the other hand there are some spots we may draw from, and I have a few suggestions to make. First I would refer to the Canadian Legion's preparedness program. I must say I think it was badly timed. That program of compulsory training in the reserve forces could not be implemented in this country for some considerable time because we do not have the facilities for training soldiers. Take a look at your reserve army set-up from Vancouver clean down to Cape Breton, and what do you see? You do not have to leave Ottawa. The barracks in this city leave much to be desired; that is about as kind as I can be. The facilities are terrible. So I think we will have to undertake a vast building program to provide barracks for reserve army training in this country, because I believe the reserve army must be the base of our army for the future. That is where the training will have to take place. I quite agree with the program of the Legion, except that I believe it was badly timed and could not be put into operation for some considerable time.
Then there is the type of training the reserve army is getting. Most of it belongs to the Boer war. They get a little bit of foot drill in the evenings. In many sections of the country you call a parade for two hours in the evening, and you will have perhaps six officers and four men turn up. Well, four men do not want to be shouted at by six officers, and the officers are in the position that they just have not the facilities; and no one is pushing the thing very hard. I believe someone will have to take a look at the whole reserve army set-up and see that it is provided with facilities so that a proper type of training may be carried on. Even the types of weapons used in the last war are obsolete today. If the reserve army is to be properly trained it should have up-to-date weapons and be taught how to use them, together with all the modern techniques. I believe training for two weeks in the summer is too short. The first week you are in camp you are busy getting the tents up and getting settled, so nothing is done. It takes three days of the second week to tear the tents down again, so they figure why bother with the remaining three days, and go have a beer. As a result not much training is done. I believe that training should be extended to at least a month.
Then I do not believe industry in this country, or even the civil service, gave proper
co-operation in permitting men to go to camp. For example, I know one industry that has a contract with its employees. If you are off a certain number of days in a month or a year you may be declared an habitual absentee and are liable to lose your employment. Men actually have lost their employment for this reason. I know some boys who went to camp last year for eight days. When they came back they were given slips notifying them that they had violated their contract and were considered habitual absentees. There is no incentive in that kind of treatment for a young fellow to take training. Worse than that, this industry pays a bonus at the end of the year. I know some young fellows who went as instructors and spent thirty days in camp. When they came back they were notified that they were absentees, so they lost 50 per cent of their yearly bonus. Someone in the government will have to check on employers of that kind. That is quite a large organization, too. I do not want to name it. That sort of thing must be corrected, however, because I believe the reserve army has to be built up as the base of our army for the future.
Then I do not want to see manpower made available in the ways I think are developing. For example, on Saturday I noticed in the press that 3,500 employees of General Motors at Oshawa had been laid off. If that kind of economic conscription is going to take place for military purposes, I think it is bad and should be clarified. No one can tell me that a shortage of materials developed so quickly that it necessitated laying off that number of men in that short time. I hope it is not a matter now of just rooting them out of what you may term non-essential industries in order to pressure them into the service. That is the worst kind of conscription, and I think the government should say this is not government policy and they are not in favour of it.
Another thing I did not like was the cutback in housing; and I see the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) is in his seat. I think that cut-back was one of the worst things that could have happened. We are going to need more and more housing. If anything serious develops which necessitates Canada making an all-out effort we are going to have to augment our manpower supply through immigration, both for military and industrial purposes, because with the manpower situation today I do not see how we can expand our economy very much and have any left to go into the services. So we may need wholesale immigration and we may need it fast. I think the cabinet did the minister a disservice wher^ they ordered him

The Address-Mr. Gillis to cut housing in this country, because I know he would not do it himself. I believe that program should have been stepped up in order to prepare for what may be an eventuality.
In my opinion this is not a situation that is going to be cleared up by tomorrow. It is a situation that is going to keep the Canadian people, and the people of this continent, on their toes for the rest of our lifetime. While we are not a military nation we have to face up to the threat from the people outside. If we let our bars down and show any signs of weakness, these people will take advantage [DOT]of it. Our only chance to keep peace in the world for any length of time is to show the other fellow we are ready to fight if he wants to fight. We are not looking for a fight, but it is being forced on us whether we like it or not. I should like the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) to take another look at the housing problem and see whether the government will permit him to go ahead with a better housing program than he had before. I am sure that if he is short of lumber the member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) and several others can tell him where to get plenty of lumber. British Columbia is full of it.
There is another way in which we could perhaps augment our labour force. There are hundreds of men in this country on pensions who are still productive, but the means test in the old age pension and war veterans allowance prevents them from taking employment. I believe the abolition of that means test in the war veterans allowance and old age pension would return to service many men who are still capable of doing some work. If the average boy drawing war veterans allowance takes a job and earns over a small amount, then his allowance is cut off. He has to go through all the red tape in order to have it restored. Most of them will just sit there. There are hundreds of men in this category who could be used, not in the heavy industries, but for replacing men who are doing light work who are capable of doing other types of work that are more essential.
For the benefit of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) I might say that there are hundreds of able-bodied men doing clerical work in the defence department who could be replaced by women. I believe the minister should take a look at that. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) enters this picture, too. Women are not going to go into industry unless there is some tax incentive given to them. If the average woman goes out and earns a few hundred dollars, her husband is declared a single man for tax purposes and ha^ to pay at that rate. I


believe that in order to augment our labour force the women should be utilized, and some compensation should be given to them if they do go to work. I believe it is necessary for everyone to get in and pitch.
On the point mentioned by the member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton), the standardization of arms, I think our men in Korea are in a spot. The United States has established and is maintaining the supply lines to Korea. If something happens to a Canadian mortar and a part is needed, they have to send to Canada for it. There is nothing in Korea. While depots have been established by the United States, our fellows cannot use American ammunition because they have different types of weapons. It is an awkward position. I do not need to tell the Minister of Finance how awkward that is. He recalls how, during the first war, we had to wait until some poor Tommy was killed in order to get his rifle because that big long pole which we had, the Ross rifle, was no good. Until we were furnished with English arms we just gathered up English equipment, and I believe that is pretty much the situation in Korea.
In my opinion the standardization of arms program should be speeded up. With all due respect for the opinions expressed by the member for Kamloops, I do not believe it is possible for us to stick to British type weapons today. The British have already agreed upon standardization with the United States. These forces are no longer the forces of any particular nation. They are the United Nations' forces. We are all in one pool. The United States has the machinery for production. They can turn it out faster than anyone else. We are all fighting together anyway, and it is just as well to have one type of equipment throughout. I believe standardization should have taken place a long time ago.
I should like to say one word on this matter of civil defence. I am not going to enlarge upon it at all because another member of this group is going to do so. Civil defence in Canada is in a pretty bad way. I believe that it is in better shape in Nova Scotia than it is in the rest of Canada. We have a very good fire marshal in the provincial government who has been working on this problem for the past two years. I believe we have pretty complete standardization of equipment in that province today, and that has to happen straight across the country. The thought I should like to leave with the minister responsible for that particular arm of defence is that, as soon as possible, civil defence should be divorced from military control. It should be organized on a local level. Villages and towns could co-ordinate in areas where they can work together. It should not be

centralized in Ottawa, and it should not be under the military arm at all. There should be a department of civil defence. During the last war in Britain it was handled almost exclusively, and very effectively, by the local authorities in the towns and villages. I believe that is the way it should be done here.
Since the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) is in his seat and has announced plans for expanding the steel industry, I should like to direct a remark to him. When I came to this house I was rather surprised that there was a shortage of steel. From discussions in this house I was under the impression right along, of course, that there was a shortage, but I read a statement made by the head of one of the large corporations in December. It was made to a yacht club, and was to the effect that there was no shortage of steel in this country. He said they could not market all the steel they were producing. It might not be a bad idea to get together with that fellow. He may be hoarding steel somewhere. If there is to be an expansion of the steel industry, as I have suggested many times in this house, the logical place for that expansion is at Sydney, Nova Scotia. There is iron ore and a supply of men at that point. You have all the facilities, coal and everything bundled together. It is a good spot for expansion. I believe the company has some plans for it, but it might not do any harm to prod them a bit.

I hope the plate mill down there has not been forgotten. The shipbuilding industry will be reopening and that mill could be used. It should be done as soon as possible.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to conclude by saying that I associate myself with the remarks made by the member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Riley) a few days ago. He made an excellent speech for the maritime provinces, and pleaded for the decentralization of industry as well as a greater recognition of the economy of those maritime provinces. Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to join with those who have taken part in congratulating the mover (Mr. McMillan) and seconder (Mr. Breton) on the excellent speeches which they made. I believe they should be congratulated on another score, for having won their by-elections. Since I came here in 1945 the history of the Liberal party in by-elections has been very bad. I
The Address-Mr. Gibson believe they must have been good men to win by the majority that they did.
I have been rather surprised that there has not been more support for this excellent brief prepared by the Canadian Legion, "Operation Preparedness". It seems to me that their suggestion that we have a national registration now is one that should be given careful consideration by the government. I realize that there are many problems and difficulties which would arise with regard to superimposing a national registration on a census, but it does not seem to me that those problems should be insuperable. It seems to me that we could use the same organization that we set up for the census in order to take this national registration. I am sure the government is giving consideration at the present time to this national registration and I sincerely trust that they will try to avoid the mistakes that were undoubtedly made the last time we had one, which was in 1941. I would presume that the government this time would be prepared to tie in our national registration with rationing.
Then there is another suggestion that also might be considered by the government, namely that it might be a wise thing if they were to consider having a fingerprint put on these national registration cards this time. We are in an entirely different type of warfare this time, and we do not want any phony registration cards running around. I would think that fingerprinting might be of great use in case there were any sabotage in the future. Certainly there are some people in this country who will object strenuously to that procedure, but my own experience has been that anyone who is an honest citizen has no hesitation about having himself positively identified under any circumstances.
The second request of the Canadian Legion is for modernization of defence resources and defence production. I believe that this brief was drawn up some time ago and that at that time there was probably some validity for the Canadian Legion's request. But after having listened to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), having seen the figures they have given us-80,000 contracts have been let for defence supplies and materials-and having had the ministers tell us what their program is to be, 1 believe that the Canadian Legion and all members of the House of Commons will be reasonably well satisfied that our government is proceeding vigorously with this particular phase of our preparedness.
276	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Gibson I now come to the third request, and many speakers have already given their views on it. I am quite sure that the Minister of National Defence is not particularly happy with the results he has obtained so far in response to his request that people should join the reserve forces. The problem is this: What is he to do about it and what assistance can we, as members of the House of Commons, be in helping the government to obtain reasonable enlistments in the reserve forces? The Canadian Legion suggests that we should have compulsory service. I realize that there are great problems in putting into effect any program for compulsory service. Immediately one brings in compulsion, one has to think about means of enforcing that policy. There is also the consideration that in large cities we have facilities such as those mentioned by the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis); we have armouries and the necessary facilities there. In the small communities, of course, we cannot have those.
I should like to see the government make some move to give the Canadian people an appreciation of the fact that we intend to try to do something about the education of our people in some form of national defence.
I do not think it particularly necessary that men should go out, put up a machine gun and take it down and have ack-ack battery practice. That in itself is only one phase of our national defence. It would seem to me that in any reserve force services we could well allow first-aid instruction, fire drill instruction, decontamination instruction-and there are many other things of that kind that would serve just as well-to give our young men in this country some useful knowledge in case they are called upon to use it.
I want to congratulate warmly the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) on what I thought was a particularly constructive speech. Whenever I hear the hon. member speak, the thought crosses my mind that he too seldom gives us the benefit of his great experience and the true wisdom that he has always displayed in this House of Commons. It seems to me that his suggestion that Canada might make her maximum contribution by concentrating more on air power than on other phases of our national defence is one that should be given great consideration by the government. From the statement made by the Minister of National Defence I can see that that is to be done.
There is another phase of national defence in which Canadians have shown particular ability, namely in our navy. I think that the contribution made by our navy in the escort service during the last war is one that contributed greatly to the allied victory.
I am sure that next time, with Russia having [Mr. Gibson.)

concentrated a great deal on submarines, Canada's defence effort could be well served if we had a competent navy such as we had in the last struggle.
I am glad to note that we had from the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg) the announcement that he was setting up a national advisory council on manpower. Knowing the minister as I do, I am quite convinced that he has no particular intention of using this body as a place to which to pass hot potatoes or anything of that kind but that he really thinks that something worth while can be done by it. The great task of this council, of course, is to try to see just how we can divert our manpower into phases that will produce greater productivity in Canada. I think the suggestion made by the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) was worth while. He suggested that possibly we could approach our labour leaders in Canada and suggest to them that they might be willing to increase the work week in this country of men working forty hours a week and that they might be willing, as part of their contribution to Canadian defence, to allow their men to work forty-four hours a week. The resulting increase in productivity would be valuable to the nation. I am also sure that the extra take-home pay these men would have would help in solving many of their financial'problems.
I think that the suggestion made by the hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough), coupled today with that of the hon. member for Cape Breton South, was a good one, namely that we should allow increased income for our pensioners and for those who are drawing war veterans' allowance. If we also allowed them to contribute to our production in Canada I think they would make a worth-while contribution because there are many skills available to us in that segment of our Canadian citizenship.
We have another source of manpower which I know the government is counting on, namely the 150,000 immigrants whom the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) has said he hoped to get into Canada this year. I sincerely trust that conditions develop which make it possible for those people to come here. After we get to that point, where do we look for the other manpower that is going to be necessary to take care of the increase we need in our production? I was going to suggest to the minister that he might consider our gold-mining industry. It has been suggested that we need gold in this country like we need a third leg in a pair of pants, and I am somewhat inclined to believe that is possibly true. We have 23,000 skilled men working

The Address-Mr. Gibson
in the industry coupled with, I should say, another 50,000 men who are probably providing them with goods and services, together with all the materials that go into the production of gold. I am quite sure that our communist friends must get quite a chuckle out of it when we have our minister of defence production get up here and tell us that he is short of critical minerals and then tell us that our greatest mining labour force in Canada is digging out gold that we take over to the border, for which we take a few American pieces of paper, and which they take and put back down in the ground in Kentucky. I am quite sure that nobody, other than on economic grounds, could suggest that that procedure even made any sense at all. It certainly does not make any contribution in Canada.

I am sure that Mr. Hitler fought quite a substantial war without having any at all. I am not sure that our Russian friends are taking any of their manpower and putting them into the production of gold, because I have never heard of Russia's gold production. We see very little of it in this country. They seem to be doing very well without it. After all, if the gold is in the mines we know it is there, and I would be quite prepared, if the gold was blocked out in the ore bodies, to support the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) if he decided to issue a certain amount of currency against the gold in the ground. It might as well be in the ground in Canada as in a cave in Kentucky.
I realize that some of our gold-mining friends in these communities which are dependent upon gold production will feel that is a very harsh suggestion to make. I am very sympathetic toward the gold mining industry. It is the one industry that has not increased the selling price of its production. Everything else has doubled and trebled in value. I would suggest that under normal circumstances we should probably revalue the price of gold and put it up to $50 an ounce. It seems to me that that amount would be much more in keeping with its true value than what it is worth at its present price, namely, $36.50 an ounce. Such a course however would be too inflationary at this time.
I was disappointed to read in the speech from the throne that the government intends to extend assistance to the gold-mining industry. I see the Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys (Mr. Prudham) in his seat. He looks a little unhappy about the suggestion of mine. I certainly hate to hand a lemon like that to a young man who has just gone into the
cabinet and is trying very hard to do a first-class job, and which I am sure he will do. However, there is one thing I would say. I am sure he would make a greater contribution to Canada's war effort if he took the manpower now engaged in gold mining and put it into the mining of strategic minerals, because I am sure there are all kinds of them in Canada that could be got out and used for national defence purposes.
There is another suggestion I should like to make but I hardly think that the government will adopt it. Any time we ever talk about anything which affects the press the government usually heads for a foxhole. The same thing is true of the opposition. It is very unpopular to do anything in this country that our friends from the newspapers do not like. I have said before that we lose millions of dollars in the Post Office Department by carrying newspapers containing the exploits of little Orphan Annie back and forth across this country at the taxpayers' expense. I do not think that it makes much of a contribution to our national welfare; but at any time that particular saving is brought up in this house everybody ducks for cover. Therefore, when I suggest that probably we are producing a little too much newsprint in Canada I wonder whether the government will go along with that suggestion either. It would seem to me that a great many of the logs that are being chewed up for newsprint could very well be turned to the production of lumber. I think probably we could get along with about half the production of newsprint in Canada that we have at the present time. Where are we sending it all? Ninety per cent of it goes down to the United States which is used of course to advertise and create a great demand for consumer goods which the United States government is trying to control. That is government policy down there. Another thing, they use it of course to produce funny papers or to glorify the Kentucky colonel, Colonel McCormick. I do not believe any of these things are essential to the prosecution of a war effort in any democratic country. If it did not mean such a tremendous waste of our great national resources and of manpower one would not object to it so much. Then there is the fact that Europe is desperately short of newsprint.
We have a story to tell in Europe. I am not too sure that some of the members of the Atlantic pact are so much sold on democracy as we should like to believe. When you come to Europe and to Great Britain you find that they have little two, three or four-page newspapers. They need more Canadian newsprint to tell a story. I do not think it is fair. I would think that

The Address-Mr. Gibson the minister of defence production or this government could enter into some kind of arrangement with the United States to cut down our shipment of newsprint to that country. Just recently I noticed an editorial in the Ottawa Journal in which it was said that one copy of a paper down in the United States had three and a quarter pounds of newsprint in it. Some of the papers in that country have a circulation of half a million. It just occurred to me that half a million of these newspapers, each weighing three and a quarter pounds, represent a million feet of timber, enough timber to build a hundred houses.
I realize that the United States must have newsprint, but at the same time it seems to me they could use it in moderation. Our government should do something about bringing it to their attention, and not let them be as wasteful as they would sometimes like to be.
There is another thing that I should like to call to the attention of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I personally was disappointed, and it was a disappointment to many people in British Columbia, when the Alberta natural resources conservation board refused a permit for the piping of gas to British Columbia. It seems to me that this is one time when selfish provincial interests should not be allowed to stand in the way of our greater national interest. I would like to feel that my good friend, the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), would discuss the matter with some of his colleagues in Alberta. After all, we might point out to them that British Columbia and Ontario also have certain natural resources. Ontario happens to have all the nickel. Ontario, therefore, might easily say, we do not want any nickel to go to Alberta. They do not need it there; we need it all here in Ontario. British Columbia has a lot of fir timber. Maybe we have not enough to spare any to Alberta. If we are to go ahead with the policy of Balkanizing Canada it will lead to disastrous results. I would certainly hope that the Alberta government-half the province out there will burn anyway in one form or another, oil, coal and gas-would show some evidence of real statesmanship, some evidence of their real concern for the welfare of Canada and try to get that gas piped out to the Pacific coast. The hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) of course is very insistent that it go through a certain pass, and I still hope that it will go that way. But before we get into any trouble I would like to have that Alberta gas in Vancouver and in the Pacific northwest.


I am glad that the Minister of Trade and Commerce is now taking on added duties. He is going to be minister of defence production, along with his other jobs. It certainly seems to me that the old adage works in the House of Commons the way it works elsewhere. You always pile a little more on the willing horse. I am certainly glad to give a man of his training and capacity the opportunity to take care of that job for us. I hope that the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) will look around that galaxy of talent that he has-all these young fellows and the older men who are willing to do so much more than they are allowed to do today. If they were to create another minister or two over there I do not think that even our financial critics would object too much to it. I hope that we do not work the senior men of the cabinet too hard; because if we should get into trouble we want their experience and advice.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce has probably heard something about the steel industry we have been trying to promote in British Columbia for a long time. I trust that he will give the matter his usual careful attention. I hope the time will come when we shall have a steel industry there. The hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) suggested that we could increase steel production in Cape Breton South. Probably we can increase our steel production in British Columbia also.
I would point out that in Comox-Alberni we have substantial deposits of high-grade magnetite ore.

speechtext:
We have a little gold out there. We will leave that in the ground for a while. We have great deposits of magnetite iron ore on Vancouver island close to tidewater. The minister does not need much coaching from me-he does very well without that-but I would certainly hope that he will see if we can get some of it into production. I do not think he will have to contribute any of Canada's money to it either, because I believe private enterprise will do it. I should like to see him facilitate in every way the use of the iron ore on the Pacific coast. I have an idea we may get some of that steel back into Canada and thus assist in relieving some of the shortages which are bound to develop.
This was not a bad speech from the throne, despite the fact that some people have said there was nothing in it. I was gratified to see that the government had come to realize the plight of pensioners in Canada. I was

The Address-Mr. Gibson
quite sure that, once the government had recognized the justice of the demand made by civil servants for increased wages to take care of the increased cost of living, it would do something for the pensioners. It must be a source of great satisfaction to those pensioners, as well as to all members in the house, that this move is foreshadowed in the speech from the throne.
The government must never forget one thing, namely the great difficulty faced by people on fixed incomes. It is good to see that those people are recognized in His Excellency's speech.
The Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) is not in the house at the moment. From various quarters of the house I have heard him criticized for having made announcements that building loans under the National Housing Act are to be cut. I do not know what measure of justification there was for his announcement, nor do I know how wise it was from a psychological standpoint. However, if one may judge from the figures placed on Hansard the other day by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), in view of the situation with respect to bathroom fixtures and soil pipe, and builder's hardware, it does not appear necessary to discourage the starting of more housing units.
However, I do not go along with what was said by the hon. and gracious member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough). She seemed to feel that because the city of Hamilton was short of houses, and because its population had increased from 150,000 to 200,000, the federal government should be primarily concerned. I think sometimes the people of Canada are inclined to believe that the government's excursion into the mortgage and building field has been such that we are now required to use reasonable prudence and businesslike judgment in how we handle matters connected with housing.
I have an idea that lending values in Canada have gone up to a pretty high point. It was made comparatively easy in this country to become a home owner. Only a small down payment was required, with the result that many people assumed mortgages far beyond* their means.
I would suggest to the hon. member for Hamilton West that at least a minor part of the housing problem could be met by the Steel Company of Canada, or the Studebaker Corporation or the International Harvester Company, or any other large company in that city. After all, if any one of them brings in a hundred new trucks as part of its operating equipment, it would have to build garages so as to keep them out of the snow. But if they bring in 20,000 extra employees, they
immediately turn to the Minister of Resources and Development and ask for houses. It seems to me that we have reached the time in this country when employers might take a little more interest in their employees' houses, and give them some assistance in that respect. I believe those companies could probably bring about some savings which private enterprise can effect much better than any form of government bureaucracy I have ever seen, or anyone else.
A number of industrial units in the logging business in my constituency have looked over the National Housing Act. They have been offered money under its provisions; but they have said, "Nothing doing. We cannot afford such a luxury, with all that red tape and regulations." I know of one outfit in my own riding that has built two hundred houses for its employees in the last four years. It was offered a government loan to the extent of $175,000 for the first one hundred units, but after looking over that offer the company decided there was too much red tape. They said that if they built the houses according to government specifications they would have to rent them for $40 a month, and that they did not believe their employees wanted to pay that much.
Instead of accepting the government money they went ahead and built their own houses. They have about two hundred of them at the present time which rent for $21 a month. The employees of that concern are ahead of the game to the extent of $19 or $20 a month. The houses are just as good as would have been built under the National Housing Act.

The small company could build three or four houses. However, I accept the hon. member's point. On the other hand most men work for some company, or work for themselves. I am not asking that the National Housing Act be discontinued, but I still think it would be an excellent idea, if, instead of shifting the problem to the municipal, provincial and federal authorities, some of the employers in the country got up and scratched for themselves, and did something for themselves once in a while, without coming here all the time asking for help.

When the house rose at six o'clock I had almost finished my remarks, but there has been so much discussion about

The Address-Mr. Gibson inflation that I think I should take a crack at that subject also. I believe anybody who really knows the situation must recognize of course that the present level of inflation in Canada and the present purchasing value of our dollar merely reflect the amount of water that the government saw fit to pump into our currency in order to win the last war. I do not think anyone in the house would blame them for the action they took at that time. After all, it was a universal method that was adopted to try to finance that great struggle.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: And nothing since then.

speechtext:
Of course it is always fashionable to look for a goat at a time like this, but I think we all must recognize what the government has done. Possibly I have been giving them a little too much praise. Once in a while they may need a little dusting-down. On the other hand, in order to be fair I think we have to recognize the fact that they have done a pretty good job since 1946 in producing balanced budgets, and indeed budgets that had substantial surpluses. Every time that those surpluses were announced there was a great deal of criticism in the house and throughout the country that the government was taking money unduly and robbing the taxpayers. I believe the very fact they did that has kept our price level within the reasonable bounds we have now.
Unfortunately our great and good neighbour to the south of us did not see fit to operate under the same kind of budgets and the effect of the good work done by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the government has been nullified almost completely by the action of the United States government in running into huge deficits at the same time. Unfortunately we in Canada cannot have a price level different from that prevailing in the United States, certainly not one which is substantially different.
It is very important that the government should address itself with real vigour and imagination to the very real problem faced by pensioners and others on low fixed incomes. I sincerely hope they will bend every effort in that direction. In due course when the Minister of Finance brings in the budget I expect that he will introduce substantial taxes on luxury goods. I think that is one way he should raise money. It is one way by which to try to discourage expenditures on non-essential items by the Canadian people. Despite the inflation everybody is talking and roaring about, I think no member of the house can stand up and say that the people of his riding are not better housed, fed and clothed, and have more economic security today than at any other time in the history of Canada.

I believe that if war is thrust upon us it will be necessary for the government to institute very definite controls in every sphere of our economic activity. When I say that I mean wage controls, rationing and the whole line-up of controls that we had in the last war. I hope the plans of the government are prepared so that they can be put into effect very rapidly if necessary. I do not want to see Canada with a menagerie of controls such as they had in the United States, rolling back prices and then rolling them up again, putting controls on and taking them off. When the government starts in to do a job of that kind I sincerely hope that they will have made up their minds and will be prepared to go ahead and make a real job of it. Until the situation develops further, I am certainly glad that we have a Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and men in his cabinet of the calibre referred to by our old friend, the great Kipling, when he says to the youth whom he is supposed to be addressing in the poem:
If you can keep your head when all about you
Are losing theirs and blaming it on you . . .

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a very great privilege for us ordinary members of the house to have the opportunity of speaking in our free parliament and expressing ourselves on problems that we feel are closely associated with our particular ridings and with the country in general. I am very glad the hon. member for Welland (Mr. McMillan) is in the house. His riding adjoins mine, and I should like to commend him highly, together with the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm (Mr. Breton) for the excellent job they did in moving and seconding the address in reply to the speech from the throne. While they were very optimistic concerning what the throne speech contained, perhaps a little more so than those of us on this side of the house, I commend them on their initial efforts.
I should like to say a word about my predecessor in office, Mr. Mark Senn, who represented the riding of Haldimand, as you know, for some twenty-eight years. I was most pleased that the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris) paid tribute to him. It was naturally not my privilege to have served in the House of Commons with Mr. Senn but it was my privilege to have lived in the riding which he represented so ably and well for a period of twenty-eight years. I can perhaps best describe the feelings of the people of the riding by telling you what a very fine old lady said when she heard Mr. Senn was going to retire from public life. She said, "Well, I guess I can go back to the party I was associated with some twenty-eight years ago."
His funeral service was attended by thousands of people from every walk of life rich

The Address-Mr. Catherwood
and poor, young and old, people who had come from far and near. One could not help but feel that we were writing the closing chapter in a book of a life of service to this country. Canada has lost a great citizen and we in Haldimand county have lost a true friend.
As I mentioned at the outset, in this debate we have the opportunity of speaking on a number of topics, and I should first of all like to say a word or two about defence. I do not expect to occupy more than twenty minutes of the time of the house this evening. According to the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton), Canada has offered to increase her air training plan for Atlantic pact allies and has invited them to train in this country. The minister has never been specific about the type of training to be provided. He has never been very specific about many other matters pertaining to national defence concerning which we would like to have information. However, he took the house into his confidence the other evening up to a certain point when he told us we were going to train 3,000 airmen in this country per year instead of the original 1,000 concerning which we previously had information. If this is to be Canada's offer, I still feel it cannot be regarded as particularly impressive. In the war of 1939 to 1945 under the commonwealth air training plan Canada trained 132,000 air crew. Among those, of course, were several thousand of our own Canadian boys. This was a remarkable achievement, and was perhaps a greater contribution to the common victory in that war than any other factor. President Roosevelt, whom we all know and recognize to have been an outstanding statesman, referred to Canada as the airdrome of democracy. Looking at our defence effort and the contributions we can make to it, it seems to me there could be no greater contribution to the cause of freedom than for Canada to offer to train air crew by the thousands, as we did in 1940-45, for the free nations joined together not only in the Atlantic pact but in the United Nations as well. The experience and knowledge gained in the commonwealth air training plan, together with the fact that many of the 154 air and ground schools are more or less intact and could be converted for training purposes, would enable Canada again to be properly called the airdrome of democracy, and to become a bulwark for the protection of free peoples against possible Soviet aggression.
Those of us who availed ourselves of the privilege of visiting the Canadair plant at Cartierville, Quebec, last week witnessed an amazing exhibition by jet fighter aircraft. We saw the F-86 Sabre travel faster than the speed of sound, between 600 and 700
miles an hour, and give a demonstration of manoeuvrability beyond what we had thought possible. If there is another opportunity I strongly recommend that hon. members visit this plant and see what this marvellous plane can do.
1 believe it is the opinion of most hon. members of this house that if a shooting war does develop air power will play a leading part, and I am entirely in accord with the view of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) and others who have given support to the need for greatly expanded air power.
It is very necessary, also, to inform our people of the great dangers with which they are faced. In a statement made some two years ago the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) said:
Recent events have brought home to us all the increasing threat to our democratic national existence of the rising tide of totalitarian communism. We know that Canada's boundaries against such a threat extend far beyond her physical frontiers. We know there can be no neutrality in this conflict.
But only last August the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson) made this statement:
The furnishing to the United Nations on short notice of expeditionary forces capable of quick deployment in distant areas wherever acts of aggression might take place had not, I admit, entered into our planning.
There is a real danger, I think, in making serious estimates of the menace of aggression and then not implementing corresponding and commensurate measures of defence. If this practice continues the conviction will gradually form in Canada that our defences, meagre though they may be, nevertheless will be sufficient to protect us and our way of life. In April 1948 the Prime Minister, speaking on foreign affairs to a Senate committee, said we were not doing enough to inform the Canadian people of what is going on. Let us implement this statement; let us frankly and truly inform the people of Canada not only of the gravity of the situation, but let it be known in plain terms what the consequences could be. That is what they want to know.
It is most encouraging to note in the speech from the throne the announcement that a department of defence production will be established to act as a procurement agency for the armed forces of our allies and ourselves. This is a department of government that I think is very necessary, and I am very glad to see it being set up. It will be openly welcomed by business generally throughout Canada. Most large industrial firms which have been working on civilian orders are ready to co-operate in industrial mobilization,
282	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Catherwood and can be depended upon to utilize their immense resources to this end when needed. Many small firms throughout the country are finding their business practically coming to an end, owing to the shortage of steel; and I believe that if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would clarify the steel situation these smaller firms might be able to stay in business.
The speech from the throne also stated we would be asked to consider measures respecting federal grants in lieu of taxation on crown properties. I am very glad the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has recognized the need for legislation of this kind and plans to bring in a measure dealing with this specific matter. I do hope serious consideration will be given the possibility of giving the municipalities power to assess all government properties within their boundaries on the same basis as other properties. I believe government property, regardless of where situated, from the largest and most extensive buildings to the very smallest, should be the responsibility of the owners, the Dominion of Canada. As the British North America Act now stands it is not possible to tax property owned by the crown.
I believe this act should be revised to make this possible. However, if the government cannot see their way clear to do so, I suggest that they consider legislation under which federal grants may be paid in lieu of taxes on all crown property. The announcement made by the Minister of Finance on November 14, 1949, in which he gave a detailed explanation of the proposed method for making grants to municipalities, was most welcome, but I think most hon. members were greatly disappointed when they learned the final details. However, now that this plan has been in operation for fourteen months I am sure the minister has learned a great deal about it, and I hope the government is now prepared to recognize the need for legislation such as I have suggested.
The speech from the throne also states that we are resolved to aid in constructive endeavours to improve the standards of human welfare in underprivileged countries. This, I believe, presents an opportunity for Canada to demonstrate to the Asiatic countries not under the Soviet heel the sincerity of our desire to aid them, by providing quantities of food and other materials. If we could see our way clear to send shipments of wheat and flour to India, Burma and other countries which would alleviate to even a small degree the hunger that prevails in those lands, I am sure we would be well repaid in the good will that would be established. I also believe that if we in the western world had recognized [Mr. Catherwood.)	i

the famine conditions which have existed in China during the past four or five years and had sent some of our surplus supplies to that country, communism would not have been the force there it is today. We cannot ignore the fact, which has been brought home to us so forcibly, that the most fertile ground for communism is in the hearts of starved and hungry peoples.
Let us hope also that at this session the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) will bring in legislation which will carry a ray of sunshine to our crippled and disabled citizens who, because of their afflictions, are unable to provide for themselves. I believe such legislation is just as necessary as that providing for aid to our blind and our old age pensioners, and just as necessary as the family allowance. Every member of this house knows of such people who are very much in need, and I feel that it is our responsibility to provide for them just as we provide pensions for our older citizens.
Along with this, on the domestic side there are no great problems requiring the attention of this house except the implementation of the social security recommendations brought before parliament at the end of the second session. It is admitted everywhere that the present old age pension plan is completely inadequate; and, since the government has expressed a willingness to act provided the provinces will co-operate by endorsing the necessary constitutional amendments, I strongly urge that the government take action on this question during this session of parliament. It is to be hoped that the government will not allow the international situation, serious though it may be, to interfere with this very necessary domestic reform. Relief for our elderly people is long past due, particularly since the inflation of the past few years has cut deeply into the purchasing power of their meagre funds. How some of these people are able to exist is beyond my imagination. I think the Minister of Finance might make use of their advice in his department.
The hon. member for Hamilton West (Mrs. Fairclough) made an eloquent plea to the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) the other evening with respect to the housing program. I certainly cannot agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson) when he says this plan should not be brought forward at this time.
I do feel that the hon. member's idea in regard to firms building homes for their employees is sound. I also feel, regardless of how many homes are built by firms, by individuals and by everyone who can possibly build, that we will still be far from having enough to supply

the demand for homes in this country, especially if we are going to continue the great immigration program that has been suggested by the government. I am heartily in accord with that program, and I believe every effort should be made to continue to expand home building in this country.
I had hoped, sir, that instead of this announcement by the minister, which cannot fail to have a depressing effect on building, a statement would have been issued to the effect that part IV of the housing act would be proclaimed, allowing for loans on home improvements. The genial Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) can win friends and influence people by influencing the government to realize the need for reconsideration of this matter.
I should like now to say a word about controls. In September of last year the government asked for and secured powers for controls. We had hoped that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) would have made a statement concerning this matter in his speech on February 8. The very least that should be done is for the government to state its intention as to whether or not controls will be introduced. As has been stated by many hon. members in this house since this session began, numerous cases have come to light in which there have been unwarranted mark-ups in the prices of a number of products by some manufacturers who anticipated government action. This increase has been and will continue to be a hedging operation against future contingencies. There can be no doubt about that. I feel that these operations will continue until some measure of controls is put into effect. The simple fact remains that uncontrolled inflation will bring disastrous results to tens of thousands of Canadian people who have practised thrift to provide for their security, and who will find that their dollar is worth approximately half of what it should be. I feel that an immediate statement from the government concerning what it intends to do about controls is necessary.
Some people have asked me what the farmers think of controls and this inflationary spiral. I can say that the position of agriculture today is affected equally by the decreased purchasing value of the dollar as are our urban friends. Dr. E. C. Hope, perhaps one of the outstanding economists in Canada, outlined the situation in an address to the Canadian Federation of Agriculture in Calgary, when he stated that the net income of the farmer reached its peak in 1944 and has since declined despite continued high prices for farm products, until today it is sixteen per cent less than in 1944. He stated, and I am entirely in accord with the main
The Address-Mr. Stick point in his address, that the responsibility and primary function of government is to protect the value of our currency. Inflation, as Dr. Hope clearly pointed out, is the last thing the farmers want. I feel, sir, that an immediate statement from the government is necessary concerning its intention with regard to controls.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, since our last session here last fall you had the honour of representing this house at the opening of the new parliament at Westminster. That you did so, sir, with honour and with dignity is a matter of satisfaction to all of us. I should like to offer you my congratulations. I should like also to join with the others who have preceded me in congratulating the mover (Mr. McMillan) and seconder (Mr. Breton) of this address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Hitherto in this house I have refrained from speaking of things provincial or things pertaining to my riding. I did so for the very good reason that I did not want my presence here to be misunderstood. The entry of my province into union was inclined to be misunderstood, and if I were to bring up provincial matters or matters pertaining to my riding, perhaps I would be misunderstood by the press of this country just as they misunderstood our entry into the union. I believe we have been here long enough now for the people of Canada to understand, so I can now revert to form and in this speech refer to matters pertaining to my province and to my riding.
The hon. member for St. John's West (Mr. Browne) has laid before this house the condition of the people in the fishing industry in Newfoundland. He did so in a very matter of fact way, and I have nothing to say in rebuttal. But I do want to say to this house that this is no new thing in the history of the fishing industry in Newfoundland. Our fishing industry, in common with all the other industries in this country, has its ups and downs. Last year we found we had a surplus of fish on our hands. When we began to market our new catch we found that this surplus brought down prices in foreign markets. That is trade as we know it in the world today. Unfortunately, the position in which we found ourselves was not kept to ourselves, but was broadcast to the four corners of the world. This did not help the industry, and it did not help us to maintain higher prices.
The fishing industry in Newfoundland is vital to the economy of the province. Hundreds of thousands of our people depend upon

The Address-Mr. Stick it for their livelihood. I make no apology tor bringing this matter to the attention ot this house, because unless we can give our fishermen the wherewithal to make a decent living this industry will decline. It will disappear from Newfoundland. Neither my province nor this country can afford to allow the fishing industry to decline in that way.
We have in Newfoundland what is known as NAFEL, which is a marketing organization that markets all of our fish. We have also a salt-cod fishing industry, and there is the federal Department of Fisheries which is represented by the fisheries board of Newfoundland. These organizations and representatives from the fishermen meet yearly, sometimes twice a year, to set the prices which the fishermen get for their catch. It is not mandatory on the purchaser to pay those prices, but I can say here that in the main the recommendations coming from those organizations are carried out. The member for St. John's West said that some of the purchasers paid too little for the fish last year. I believe that to be correct. But I would also like to say that on other occasions they paid more than the price recommended by these organizations.

May I ask
a question? Is it not a fact that this year the joint committee to which you referred did not set the price for fish?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
They did not this year, but they have in the past. The situation in Newfoundland is something we have had for many, many years. It cannot be cured overnight, and it did not come overnight. I suggest to this house that instead of blaming the purchaser or blaming NAFEL or other organizations in Newfoundland, all these organizations should get together in a spirit of good will to ascertain what is wrong with the industry and devise ways and means whereby this industry could be put on its feet. I believe that is a reasonable and sensible way of going about it. I believe a solution of our problem could be found in that manner.
You may be inclined to ask, who are these people about whom I am speaking? Are they worthy of assistance? Let me tell you in all sincerity that these people in Newfoundland who get their daily bread by toiling on the sea, and who face the Atlantic in its calm moods and in its stormy periods, are producing some of the things which you eat here. It is necessary for the economy of this country that we keep the fisheries going just as much as it is necessary to keep the farming industry going. Those men are brave. They face the dangers of the sea day and
[Mr. Stick.)

night. They know what it is to be on the Atlantic when storms are raging, and when the wives and the children at home are praying that they may return safely. Those are the men that helped to keep the Atlantic sea lanes open so that your commerce could travel to and from Europe during the first world war. Those are the men who beat the U-boat menace on the Atlantic during the last war. Those are the men who are today enlisting in the Royal Canadian Navy in such large numbers. They are the men that Churchill called for during the second world war when he wanted men to man the small boats of the Royal Navy. He sent out a special call for them, and he named them the greatest small-boat men in the world. If we get into a shooting war they will respond again as they have in the past. They are willing. I speak on their behalf tonight, and I make no apology for doing so.
For fifteen years in Newfoundland we had a form of government that we called a little dictatorship. You may call it bureaucratic, if you like. We know what we suffered under that regime. In my riding we know how the wharves, the navigation aids and public works generally deteriorated. They were not kept up and they withered as grapes on the vine. I have made recommendations here in all honesty and in all sincerity, which were designed to assist the people about whom I am speaking tonight. I ask for special considera*-tion on behalf of those people. Since I have come here, particularly lately, I have found a certain amount of the bureaucratic business that we had in Newfoundland years ago. We now find that all requests going in are answered with one word "no", that defence comes first, and that we must economize. I would say that there is such a thing as false economy. When those requests are taken into consideration, I hope that those people who live hundreds and thousands of miles from the sea will realize how the people for whom these requests are made earn their daily bread. It requires no brains to say "no". You can teach a parrot to say that. In bringing this matter before the house on behalf of those people I ask, in all sincerity, that they be given the consideration which they deserve.
There is one other matter, Mr. Speaker, which I should like to bring to the attention of the house at this time; perhaps I should say there are two matters, but one is interwoven with the other. Recently we have heard of the huge iron ore deposits in Labrador. It is necessary for the economy not only of Canada but of the whole North American continent that that iron ore be placed in the hands of the steel makers so that we may have the requirements of steel

The Address-Mr. Drew
to meet our needs. That development will take place in two or three years. In two or three years that ore will be coming up and going through the steel furnaces in the middle west and other parts of Canada. I want to make a plea here tonight for the deep water canal on the St. Lawrence seaway.

speechtext: We are right with you on that.

speechtext:
When the fathers of this nation looked out upon this country they saw vast tracts of land inhabited by people who were scattered. They conceived the idea of welding this country into one nation and they did it by building railroads. We have advanced from that stage, and last year we had in this house legislation respecting what is known as the trans-Canada highway. That is to further the process of cementing this country into one nation. I submit that today the St. Lawrence seaway is vital not only to the defence of this country but to its economy. Far too long have we waited for our friends and neighbours to the south of us while this project was kicked around as a political football. The time has come when we must act and, if necessary, do so alone. I am informed that this project will cost from $700 million to $800 million and that it will take some four to five years to complete it. In spite of what has been said here in this house this afternoon by the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sinclair), I am convinced that it is within the capacity of this country to carry out that project, if necessary, alone. I am further convinced that the time to begin it is now. We will welcome our friends in the United States if they come in with us but I say here definitely tonight that we cannot wait longer than 1951 and that we must be ready to begin this project in 1952 even if we have to go it alone.
Last year some of us paid a visit to Windsor and Detroit. We saw the huge industries in that area. Those of us who like the sea and who have the sea in our blood were naturally interested in the water. We saw the huge amount of shipping passing to and fro on that strip of water between Windsor and Detroit, and we were told that that stretch of water has on it the greatest amount of sea traffic in the world, that the amount of shipping passing up and down that river is far greater than that passing through the Suez canal or the Panama canal. From looking at it at the time, I can well believe that statement. I myself have been through the Suez canal on four or five occasions. I have been on defence for two or three months on the Suez canal and I know what traffic goes through it. I ask the house to visualize
what will happen when we get that deep water canal on the St. Lawrence. I say that the traffic passing between Detroit and Windsor can be duplicated on the St. Lawrence and that this seaway will knit this country as it has never been knit before. It will allow the resources of the east to flow to the west and the resources of the west to flow to the east. It will be one other link binding this country together.
We have at this time the spectacle of the shortage of steel. Almost every day in this house we receive new orders with respect to the curtailment of the use of steel. We have the iron ore in Labrador; we have the coal in the maritime provinces, and we have the limestone. Why have we not the steel industry today capable of supplying our needs? I ask this house to have vision and faith. It has been said that as goes the family, so goes the nation. Carved in letters of stone in the peace tower, at the western end, are these words:	Where there is no vision, the people
perish. This chamber here represents the family of Canada. Our forefathers supplied the faith and the vision to make this country great. Is it too much to ask of us here now that we supply the vision necessary to make those projects I have mentioned come to fruition? Inasmuch as our forefathers by their vision made Canada great, is it too much to ask of each one of us here tonight that we carry on in our day and generation the example they set and that we make Canada greater?
