speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before I proceed
with my other remarks, may I say I understand that some remarks were made this afternoon which were intended for my particular attention. All hon. members are well aware of the sad event which kept me away from this house on Thursday and Friday. For that reason it was necessary for me to take some time this afternoon to examine Hansard so that I might know what had been said during my absence. I regret that I did not have the opportunity to hear the remarks to which I have referred. I trust that those remarks were a serious attempt to examine the grave problems now before us.
We are now discussing the amendment moved by the opposition and the subamendment which was moved to that amendment, and which adopted the wording of the amendment, making the additions now under consideration. I think I might read into the record at this point the words of the amendment and the subamendment so that we shall have before us exactly what it is that we are

The Address-Mr. Drew considering in this debate at this very important time. This is the amendment:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed
(1)	to give this nation leadership in the face of the present grave danger; and
(2)	to bring into being forces necessary to enable Canada to defend itself and discharge its international obligations; and
(3)	to take effective measures to combat inflation and the rapidly rising cost of living.
A subamendment was moved to that which reads as follows:
That the following words be added to the amendment, immediately after the words "rising cost of living" in the last line thereof:
"such as the immediate reimposition of price controls, and the payment of subsidies where necessary, so as to protect the health and living standards of the Canadian people.
That is what we have under consideration; and the vote that will be taken at the time it is called will be upon that amendment, accepted in the subamendment, with the additional words that I have just read.
Before I come to the subamendment I should like to deal with the first two subjects mentioned in the amendment which I moved in the early stages of this debate. It covers three subjects. First, the failure of the government to give leadership in these critical days. Second, the failure of the government to bring into being the defence forces required to fulfil our tasks at this particular time; and third, the failure of the government to deal with the high cost of living and inflation.
First of all, let me deal with the question of leadership or lack of leadership given by the government at this time. After all, on an occasion when we are told that we face as grave dangers as ever confronted western civilization, it is most certainly imperative that the government give leadership to the people of this country as to the nature of the tasks that they must undertake, and as to the way in which they can best contribute to the common effort to be made by all our people.
If there had been any question in the opening stages of this debate about the complete absence of leadership by this government that doubt must have been removed during the course of this debate from anyone who is prepared to examine carefully exactly what the government has put before us during the past two weeks.
First of all, we had a statement by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) which indicated what might be done if, as and when the government thought there was any reason to act. Then we had a statement by the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) in regard to the money to be spent; and we had placed before us, in a cumulative form,

an estimated total of the amount which might be spent over a period of three years. I would remind hon. members that our obligation, our duty and our only right is to deal with the things that will be dealt with in the coming year, although I agree that it is wise to plan for the time ahead.
We knew in advance of the statement by the Minister of National Defence that approximately $1,600 million was to be spent on defence during this current year. What was told us then was not new. It is only a question of simple arithmetic to reach the conclusion that carried forward over a period of three years it would approximate $5 billion. There is not a single member in this house, including the Minister of National Defence, or the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), or the Prime Minister, who has the slightest idea of what the expenditure may be that this country will be called upon to meet if events during this current year should take the course that presented us with graver dangers than those we now face. The whole presentation of this subject was placed before us as though we were in a period of relatively stable preparation for defence, in spite of the fact that we have been told by the government that the next few months may be the most critical in the history of the western world.
Again, the announcements that were made indicated an approach on a long-term basis to the provision of manpower and of weapons, and of the things that are required for the defence of this country. Money is very necessary in preparing for military defence. This parliament and the people of this country have learned that it takes a great deal of money in a free nation to bear the burden of defence. But the actual burden of defence itself is not the dollars that are put forward. Defence rests upon trained men with weapons with which they can defend our freedom.
What we need to know, if the crisis is in the nature of the crisis that has been described to us, is how many men fully trained and equipped and armed this country is going to have on April 1, on May 1, on June 1, on July 1, on August 1, on September 1, during the most critical months that the western world will face for many years. There is nothing in what has yet been placed before us that gives us any real indication of what measures of defence this country actually has, or will have, during these most critical days.
There was one speech from the government benches which approached this subject in an atmosphere of reality-and only one. That was the speech of the hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power). In that speech a man.

who had accepted the responsibility of one of the defence ministries during the years of war pointed out the obligation that there is on every member of the House of Commons to know what we actually have to defend this country.
He himself, not unnaturally, indicated his own interest and his own faith in that branch of the service with which he was associated during the years of war. He presented to us reasons why he thought this country should place the utmost emphasis upon the Royal Canadian Air Force and upon the training and equipping of air units. He suggested that members of the house should express their opinions as to the balance of emphasis which should be placed upon one branch of the service and another.
I for one wish to subscribe to the views he expressed, that there are reasons that Canada is peculiarly fitted and qualified to train large numbers of airmen, and that our greatest emphasis should be upon that branch of defence. For at least two years to my recollection the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) has been urging that greater emphasis be placed upon air defence; and I am very happy to see that an increasing measure of emphasis is placed upon this service.
I think our geographical position suggests reasons why we can best contribute both to the defence of Canada and any collective effort that may be made, either in Europe or any other part of the world, by those military craft that can move so fast into any area of danger.
There is another reason-and I should like to indicate that this is no new conviction of mine, but rather one I have held for many years. Like the hon. member for Quebec South, I have sought for some time to emphasize the special qualifications possessed by Canadians in this great branch of the military service. In 1930 in a book I wrote under the title "Canada's Fighting Airmen" I had this to say about the particular qualifications of Canadians in this field:
Canada's share individually and collectively was out of all proportion to her population. Not long after Canadians really took up flying in earnest it became apparent that they were at least the equals of any of the airmen in the war. It is interesting to speculate why they displayed such an undoubted superiority in this new service. There must be some explanation for the fact that Canada, with about one-tenth of the white population of the empire, should have supplied one-third of the pilots in action with the Royal Air Force at the end of the war, and there must also be some explanation for the individual dominance of Canadians among the British fighting pilots. Perhaps the wide horizons of life in Canada, the atmosphere of optimism, the confidence of individual opportunity, and the general adaptability to unexpected tasks bom of life in a rapidly developing country all contributed to the
The Address-Mr. Drew qualities which so peculiarly fitted Canadians for success in this new and incalculable adventure. Whatever the reasons may have been, the simple fact remains that, without any qualification as to population or otherwise, Canadians proved themselves the greatest air fighters on the side of the allies. Their exploits should be an inspiration to young Canadians for all time, because at the height of their glory these men were mere boys, and what Canadian boys did then forever avoids the necessity of seeking beyond the borders of Canada for examples of the highest bravery, devotion to duty and self-sacrifice.
Those same qualities were shown during the second world war. Those same qualities are possessed by young Canadians today, and I think there are good reasons why the utmost emphasis should be placed upon this service. There are also reasons why emphasis should be placed upon the equipping and training of airborne troops. There are also reasons why emphasis should be placed upon the equipping and training of fast armoured units which can train in the great spaces of this country and be moved rapidly into any threatened area. There are also reasons why, with our great coast lines, and the fact that there is good reason to believe that the danger spots where trouble might arise may be some distance from our own shores, we should build ships of a type which would make it possible for those young men and women who have shown such great adaptability for naval service to continue that service wherever Canadians may be required to assume the collective responsibilities they have accepted.
Then we come to the land forces. In that we still depend to a very considerable extent upon the reserve army, which can be organized here in Canada and can be brought into a position to defend this country during a period when any threat might present itself.
No one should underestimate the importance in the Canadian defence plan of the reserve army. One of the things that have not been answered in the debate, but which should be answered, is the statement by the senior officers of all the associations representing the different branches of the land forces, that any suggestion that the number of men we have in the reserve is an effective force for the defence of this country is a travesty of the facts. These men who made that statement are the men who know best of all what the state of training of the reserve units really is. They know better than the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton). They know better than the general staff. They know better than anyone else because they are the ones who are actually assuming responsibility for that training. They have made the bald statement that we are not getting full value for our money in reserve

The Address-Mr. Drew
training, and that any statement that we have 40,000 effectives, which has been made over and over again, is a travesty of the facts.
This is not a time for us to be given any statements which do not clearly and accurately represent the situation with which we are confronted. Examine the speech of the Minister of National Defence. It tells us how much money the government may spend. It tells us what units may be raised with the money to be spent, assuming that it is still dollars of the same kind. It tells us also some of the general plans, but it does not tell the members of the house what the defence forces are that we have today, what the state of our defences actually is, how ready we are to meet any threat that might confront us, or how ready we are to accept our share in any collective responsibility that we have assumed.
The hon. member for Quebec South (Mr. Power) raised an extremely important point when he said that one of the great problems confronting us now, when so much power of necessity is assumed by this and other free governments in the face of threats of this kind, is to find a method by which members of parliament can be fully informed and assume the responsibility which it is their duty to assume before they pass the votes of money which they are called upon to pass. The hon. member for Quebec South supported the idea of a committee to examine defence so that members might be informed. He pointed out that such a committee should not be permitted to deal with questions of policy. I agree with that. At no time have I suggested that a committee should deal with questions of policy. Policy must be the exclusive responsibility of the government. What I have urged is that there be a committee which can examine the facts so that in turn the committee may report to the house and the house may know what the state of the defences of this country really is in these most critical days.
In the various things that have been said, suggestions have been made that staff officers be called before that committee, and if in any of those statements the government has interpreted the argument as an argument that such a committee be permitted to deal with questions of policy, may I remove any suggestion of that kind. The suggestion has been made, and my argument now is, that such a committee is essential if members of the house are to have the facts in regard to defence which they should have if they are in fact going to perform their duty and their responsibility as representatives of the people of Canada at this time. Short of that we have no adequate information. Short of that we are passing over this great subject with 

a statement as to the amount of money to be spent. What do members of this house know about the state of our active force? I have sought to ascertain what the state of our active force is, that almost forgotten force which was by-passed when it came to the acceptance of responsibilities under the United Nations, that magnificent well-trained force.
Do not let members of this house be asked to accept the explanation that the airborne brigade was kept in Canada to defend Canada in the event of attack. The aircraft which could have carried the airborne brigade into action were sent outside of Canada, and they cancelled their training last autumn because of that fact. Today we have land forces of at least three different types. We have the special force; we have the active force, which seems to be particularly for the defence of Canada; and we have the reserve force, as well as such other forces as might be brought into existence. Surely members of the house have a right to hear a discussion of this subject and opinions expressed as to the organization of military forces which will most effectively deal with the tasks before us.
That is not a question of government policy. It is a question of the presentation of facts upon which members of the house can then make their arguments as a result of which the government in turn would decide policy, which is its responsibility. Most certainly the thing that is creating an atmosphere of uncertainty and confusion in Canada today is the absence in the house or outside of that detailed information which is so essential if we are going to assume our responsibilities. For that very reason I once again repeat my earnest request to the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) that the government agree to set up a committee to examine the whole subject of national defence, recognizing that there will be subjects that must be kept behind the veil of secrecy but recognizing also that this house is always ready to accept any reasonable explanation in that respect, and has never sought to violate the secrecy essential in cases where real secrecy is needed.
When it is suggested that this would be taking over the responsibility of government, may I once again point out that surely external affairs are just as much in the realm of secrecy as national defence, that a committee is set up to deal with that subject, and that it has never been suggested at any time that the external affairs committee is usurping the authority of parliament. There is plenty of evidence of what has been accomplished by committees in other countries. I have been told by those in a position to know-and I am sure other members of the house have

received the same information-that one of the reasons that little Finland was able to make such a magnificent stand against Russia in 1939 was because a committee of their parliament had been set up to examine national defence, and that committee made recommendations which led to a reorganization of the defence forces of Finland as a result of which we had that sublime act of courage when that little nation stood against the full force of communist slavery. We would reap the same benefits. We would receive information to which we are entitled, and I hope that, at this stage of the session, when it is so important that we proceed with knowledge of the subject we are discussing, a committee of that kind will be set up.
Then let us examine the information placed before us by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). Surely there was a complete absence of leadership there. If any member of this house knows definitely any more than he did before that speech, he has been able to find in it something I could not find. That speech was simply a statement that certain things may be done some time; that some things are under serious consideration. This is a time for serious consideration, Mr. Speaker, but it is also a time for action; and the time for action is long past in regard to some of the subjects that were discussed by the minister.
One of the most remarkable things to have been presented during this debate, either inside or outside the house, is the suggestion that it is not necessary for us to tackle some of these problems because the people of the United States are also tackling them and this may be adequate for our requirements. Surely the sovereignty of this country, the sovereignty of this parliament, suggest that no member of the Canadian government should stand in this house and say he expects that the things done by some other nation are going to be adequate to deal with the problems we are called upon to face. This parliament has the responsibility of dealing with its own problems. Today as we prepare for defence, as the enormous sums of money that will be called for will be spent, we know that the inflationary pressures in the country will be infinitely greater than they are at present. We know we have not yet even felt some of the inflationary pressure already created. We know some raw materials are going into industrial production which cannot be replaced at the same price. We know that when those raw materials must be replaced the prices will go still higher, simply from the evidence of what those raw materials cost today. We have seen what has been happening in connection with inflation. We know 80709-19
The Address-Mr. Drew how it has been increasing, and we also know the whole tendency will be for it to increase still further unless effective steps are taken to bring it under some measure of restraint.
It is not necessary to remind some members of this house of what has happened; nevertheless it is important that we all bear in mind what has been taking place during the past few months. In 1949 the cost of living index had risen to 160-8 and people were getting seriously concerned about it. For the last month of 1950 it had climbed to 171-1. During the twelve months of 1950, the cost of living climbed 11-5 points, or practically one point a month. Some of the statements being made on behalf of the government gave us every reason to hope that this tendency had been checked, but the latest bulletin issued on February 2 of this year shows that the general cost of living index is now 172-5. The government has given some indication that it may deal with this subject by controls, but it is not yet prepared to say exactly what it is going to do or what form the steps it has under serious consideration may actually take.
Today, Mr. Speaker, we are not dealing simply with a cost of living index as such. We are dealing with a situation that is threatening the people of this country with a measure of insecurity they have not known for many years, a measure of insecurity in no way related to the apparently high income our people are earning at the present time. One of the things that must be borne in mind in all these discussions is that it is no use talking about the high national product in terms of dollars unless we talk about that national product in terms of what those dollars will buy, and what kind of dollars they really are. After all, the national product of France today in francs is many times what it was in 1914; the national product of Italy is many times what it was in 1914, in lira; but it is a very different figure when you examine those units in terms of money value today, and in what they will buy. What has been happening in Canada in the past few months should be an indication and a warning that here, as in other countries, that same dangerous course may be run unless with all the vigour, all the ingenuity and all the initiative we possess we deal with the emergency that is actually upon us in regard to the cost of living.
There is no one here who does not know from his own personal contacts the desperate position in which many people are living today. A man earning $120 a month may be called upon to pay $50 or $60 for rent if he has a family. He may be called upon to buy fuel in addition to that, and then food. Where

The Address-Mr. Drew the money is to come from for clothes and all the other incidentals is hard for anyone to imagine. Yet that is the reality with which we are actually confronted at this time. This government, through its lack of leadership, is primarily responsible for the inflation we see in Canada today. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) laughs. This is not a laughing matter. Certainly it is not a laughing matter to the people who are trying to find out how to make their dollars go around at this time. It is not a laughing matter for the people to have invested money in insurance for their own protection, and who know that the dollars they get from that insurance are worth only a little more than fifty cents as compared with the dollars they put in.

This is not a laughing matter for those who have put their money in the banks in the form of deposits, in order to protect themselves. Nor is this a laughing matter for those who have put their money in government bonds which they have been told was the safest form of investment into which they could put their money. The Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) says that he is laughing at the suggestion that the government was responsible. The government is responsible. The government has not taken one single step, since the pressures were placed upon the economy of this country, to check inflation by any of the several measures they could have taken to deal with this subject.
Mr. Speaker, I know that those people of Canada who are concerned about the value of money today will be interested to know that this is such a humorous subject to some of the members on the government side. This government had it in its power to do a number of things that would have greatly helped to meet this situation. Those things were pointed out many times. One step that was suggested was that the government cut down on non-defence spending. Those members who have an interest in the affairs of parliament, and who follow the debates in parliament, will know that it was in this parliament that the suggestion was made that, if savings were effected here comparable to those indicated in the United States by a similar commission, they could amount to $500 million a year in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, there are certain members in this house who know nothing better than to laugh, and who have made no better contribution.

But, Mr. Speaker, it is only an attempt to be doctrinaire from another point of view to suggest that there is a free economy in which the movement of prices, on a competitive basis, offers protection to the public when any large part of the basic commodities, supplies or production of any kind is bought by the government for special purposes with the money appropriated by this house, and that much of that production or of those commodities is removed from the ordinary free competition within this country. The moment that any substantial part of any commodity or of any type of production is bought directly or indirectly by the government, then the free economy is no longer operating in relation to the balance of those supplies. Any failure to take effective steps to deal with the balance of those supplies is simply playing into the hands of the speculators and those who will be able to make money at the expense of the general public. I believe that our free economy may be gravely threatened, and soon, unless this runaway inflation is brought under control. I for one believe that it is essential that, to meet this immediate emergency, there be price controls which will protect the public from the abuses that are arising at this time.
By all means let us have the highest measure of freedom within this economy of ours, but let us face the simple reality that the water is running over the dam so fast that unless flood gates are provided right away this flood may carry away the savings of our people and that free economy which is being asserted as the reason for not doing anything at this time. After all, communism can win this struggle in more ways than by force of arms. That has been said in this house before. Communism has already extended its dreadful slavery to large parts of the world without moving a single armed man across the borders where communist dictatorships have been set up. There are other ways that communism can be spread; and one of the ways that the communists have said they would seek to spread their dreadful disease is by undermining the economy of the free nations so that the destruction of that economy would open the door to this dreadful form of slavery that they are trying to impose upon the whole world.
People did not believe Hitler when he wrote in "Mein Kampf" exactly what he intended to do, namely, to enslave Europe and the rest of the world, and too late the world came to realize that he meant exactly what he said, and that he intended to carry out that plan. Stalin has told us in just as clear
[Mr. Diew.l	.
terms what he and the Russian dictatorship intend to do. They plan to extend their control over the whole world; not so much by force of arms as by the threat of force against countries where the economy has been undermined through the many activities that they carry out.
Every point that our cost of living goes up is something that will bring satisfaction in the Kremlin. I would not be surprised' if on the walls of the Kremlin, probably opposite the walls where they have all the maps of free nations they have absorbed in other ways, are charts showing the dangerous trend in the free nations and the threat that there is to the free economies which they are seeking to destroy. It is just as important in this country today to protect our dollar, the dollar which our people need for their daily lives, for their savings and for their security, as it is to build the bulwarks of freedom of other kinds. Neither can be neglected. Both these great efforts should go on side by side and simultaneously, and the time to deal with the threat to our economy is now long overdue.
In so far as our amendment is concerned, Mr. Speaker, it was intended to cover the field of inflation. We express regret that the government had failed to take effective measures to combat inflation and the rapidly rising cost of living. These are inclusive terms. Certainly these terms include price controls where price controls are necessary. Certainly, these words include subsidies where subsidies are necessary. But they include several other things as well. To any of those who may find some measure of amusement in an assertion of that kind, may I point out that I had the responsibility-and I accepted it-of introducing certain subsidies in the province of Ontario at a time when the dominion Minister of Agriculture was failing to protect certain of our important crops that faced a very dangerous situation indeed.
For instance, in Ontario we found it necessary to provide a subsidy for sugar beets, a subject of which the Minister of Agriculture has had some recent experience. This of course was on an earlier occasion. There was a serious shortage of sugar in this country at that time and the production of sugar beets was seriously threatened. I have no apologies for accepting the responsibility of introducing a subsidy to continue the production of that crop, while at the same time I disbelieve in the general principles of subsidies except where they are actually needed to meet an emergency of this kind. We introduced subsidies to assist hog production, to assist cheese production and to assist production of other kinds.

I have had experience in this before, and I know there are occasions where the nature of the emergency demands that we deal with these things in terms of reality and meet the situation head-on, and do the things that are needed to be done to deal with the problem that is before us.
In this subamendment there are the governing words, "if necessary". And that is exactly the meaning that I take from these words. But if it had been intended to amplify the words in our motion we would have amplified them a great deal more than this. The fact that we have not, however, does not make the reference to these objectionable; because quite contrary to what some hon. members have suggested, this subamendment does not leave the whole question of inflation upon these two subjects alone. It says: "such as price controls and subsidies where necessary".
Much has been made of the words, "reimposition of price controls". I grant you that I do not like the word "reimpose"; but what is it that we are talking about? We are talking about price controls, but not necessarily price controls of the same kind that we had before. No; Canadians have got too much initiative, too much ingenuity, too much intelligence not to have gained a great deal from the experience of the last war. And in dealing with the problems now before us under different circumstances, and meeting a longterm situation, I am perfectly certain that the price controls that would be devised to meet the emergency with which we are now confronted would be a different type of price control from those that were imposed before. But I am not going to engage in an exchange of dialectics and argument about whether some inference can be drawn from the word "reimpose".
This refers to price controls; this refers to subsidies. It leaves it open to deal with any other things than can be done to stem inflation in this country. I am going to point out some of the other things that are covered under these general terms that were used in our amendment. First of all is the reduction of non-defence spending by this government, and a substantial reduction of non-defence spending. Second is increased production in every line of production which will not only meet our military requirements, but which will meet the daily needs of our people and by that very fact ease the strains and pressures of inflation itself. And third, we should encourage immigration on a scale which will bring to our country people with skill and stamina who believe in our methods, so that we may spread the burden we have assumed over a larger population within this vast land of ours. And fourth, we should most certainly remove anything that will
The Address-Mr. Drew discourage the people from building houses at a time when we are also encouraging immigrants to come into this country.
Anything more badly conceived than the plans of the government to reduce demand by creating the necessity for a higher down payment would be difficult to imagine. We have no lack of raw materials in this country. We have no lack of resources. We have resources in this country beyond the dream of most nations in the world today. What we need at this time is for this government not to place restrictions upon the building of houses at the very time that we are trying to convince the people that our way of life is the best of all, but to encourage them to build houses where you create the whole foundation of your society.
Then again another point is that this house should insist upon every step being taken which will assure that we get full value for every dollar spent on defence. This house should insist upon every step being taken which will assure that we get full value for every dollar spent on defence. We know we are not getting it today.
Then we should also demand, with the hope that this demand would not be confined to one side of the house, that the government use the very wide powers it has to deal with the credit of this country. After all the Bank of Canada was set up with its very first declared purpose being the supervision of the credit and economy of the country to the best advantage of the people of Canada. The government, through the agencies it has created, has it within its powers to do several things that will help to prevent this runaway inflation that is now before us.
Then again we come to the question of controls. Most certainly we urge that, to meet this emergency with which we are now confronted, there be controls, where those controls are needed, to bring the dollar into some real relationship to a proper value, and to create a measure of stability which will restore the confidence of the people of this country in their bank savings, in their insurance, in their bonds, and in other things which are so necessary if we are going to carry forward a free economy.
Surely the government should be very conscious of the danger there would be in putting out a bond issue by the government to meet our defence requirements, unless there was some measure of assurance that the people who put up their money are going to have reason to believe that it will be at least a somewhat similar dollar they will get back when those bonds mature.

The Address-Mr. Drew
That is not suggesting that the people of our country are going to reduce their patriotism to dollars. But at a time when the government is urging the people to put money into those bonds as the safest investment in the country, then the government has the responsibility to make them the safest investment. The fact is that they have not been the safest investment, and that during these past few years-during this past year particularly-there has been a real threat to investment in those bonds, which is now a subject which should cause serious concern to the government and to the people of Canada.
In passing I shall refer to another subject not unrelated to investments. The stock markets of Canada serve an important and useful purpose. In a free economy those stock markets provide the opportunity to buy and sell securities which finance the great developments under our economy. There are still people who express some measure of surprise that at a time when events are undoubtedly serious the stock markets should be rising, rising, rising, to a point where it is strangely reminiscent of the days of 1929. Why is that? Is it because the people of Canada are confident that these stocks are worth more every day? Some of them, yes. But the real reason that there has been this constant and rapid rise is the concern of many people as to the continuing value of the dollar; and they are putting their money into what may be regarded as equity securities which bear a proportionate relationship to some fixed assets which change with the changing value of the dollar. And yet part of the increase in the value of securities in this country has been an increase that has been related to a flight from the dollar itself-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Nonsense.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
And I hear the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) say "nonsense." If any word could demonstrate how unfitted he is to be Minister of Finance, it is that word. The Minister of Finance obviously does not read the financial papers which are subscribed to by the people employed in his own department to give expert advice. The minister is disregarding what is being said by those who have been observing this phenomenon for some time; and the minister knows perfectly well that in other years, as well as this year, when there is inflation in this country or in other countries, there is a corresponding increase in stock values related to the fact that inflation itself carries those values up. In that, of course, I am referring to common stocks, because it is the common stock which has the equity value in the assets of any company.
[Mr. Drew.)

It is time that, in addition to urging there be some effective measure of control over those things which are threatening our economy, the people of this country should also come to realize that there is no easy way to wealth, that real wealth is earned only by hard work, by initiative and by ingenuity. And it will be a healthy thing in this country if some measure of caution is displayed by the people at this time, and that they should not believe that the stock markets in Canada or in any other country always go one way. Because, while it would be certainly very unwise that anyone should ever sell Canada short, it would also be unwise that the people of this country should come to regard stock exchanges as gambling casinos where they are simply tossing money down for chips of one kind or another which they buy and put on some gambling device. That is not what stock markets are. Stock markets provide a very real and important function in our economy. Their place will best be held and the service they can offer will best be performed when everyone recognizes that the value of those exchanges should be related to the actual value of a security itself, and related to the production of any particular company.
I come now to the question of how these things can be done. If the government does adopt a stabilization policy, if the government does make a real effort to stabilize the dollar, controls alone will not do the job. Controls alone might only aggravate the situation and create new problems in years ahead. The whole problem must be tackled, along with imposing those restraints and controls made necessary by the action of the government itself. And the government should also take these other steps which can be taken for the benefit of all the people of this country.
I spoke about the necessity for increasing production. Taxes imposed should be taxes which will encourage savings. Taxes imposed should be taxes which will in every way possible not stifle the productive capacity and productive effort of this nation. There are taxes which can be borne by the people of this country without placing any shackles upon the great productive capacity of Canada. There are other taxes which would greatly reduce our ability to meet the demands ahead. The mainspring of a free economy-and it is a free economy in which I believe and a free economy which I hope we will preserve-is the hope of getting more in the form of money or goods or other things for the efforts that are being made, and of being able to create security, comfort and happiness for your family by saving from what you earn. If the

safety of bank deposits, insurance, government bonds and other investments of our people is threatened, then in doing so the very mainspring of our economy is threatened as well. In imposing the taxes that will be imposed upon the people of this country to meet the heavy demands ahead, every single thing should be done to see that they are imposed in a way that will make it possible for production to meet the demands of our people while at the same time meeting defence requirements.
For that very reason it is to be hoped that the government will give an opportunity to the house at the earliest possible date to deal with the estimates, to examine them and to see what actually can be done, by suggestion and otherwise, to improve the situation. I have directed criticism to what I believe the government has failed to do. But to the extent that the government really meets its responsibilities, to the extent that this government really shows a determined effort to stem the tide of inflation, I am sure they will get the support of every member of the house no matter what criticism may have been directed to what has taken place in the past.
For the reasons I have mentioned it is my intention to support the amendment to the amendment. In doing so I have indicated that the subjects discussed are subjects to which we have referred. If I had drafted the subamendment I might have changed the wording of it, and would; but what I point out is that the one way in which members of the house have an opportunity to protest against the inaction of the government is to vote on a subject of this kind without too much attempt to get down to the last possible meaning of every word in the amendment to the amendment now before us. I hope that it will not only be members on the opposition side of the house who will indicate to the government that they want some action, because I know, and every member of the house knows, that there are members on the government side as well who believe that conditions in this country today are such that they demand immediate and vigorous action, and that the urgency which has been suggested is not only an urgency related to defence preparation but also is a great urge^y related to the preservation of our free economy and the welfare of our people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it would seem appropriate at this point that I should say something on the third point in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew). The amendment reads in part:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed . . .
The Address-Mr. Abbott
(3) To take effective measures to combat inflation and the rapidly rising cost of living.
At the same time it will afford me the opportunity of accepting a suggestion that was made in my absence the other evening by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green). At page 165 of Hansard he said:
I also believe that it would be most opportune if the Minister of Finance were to make a full and frank statement in this debate on ways to prevent inflation. I realize that price controls are not a cure-all, but I believe it is the duty of the Minister of Finance to tell the house, and through us the Canadian people, everything that can be done. There is little understanding throughout the country of the underlying causes of inflation or of the best remedies. We hear, for example, such recommendations as these: that individuals should increase their personal savings, that the government should cut out every unnecessary expenditure, that there should be heavier taxation, that there should be restriction of credit, that there should be an allocation of scarce materials, that interest rates should be raised so that persons having savings accounts, for example, would receive a higher rate of interest and thus would be encouraged to save rather than spend; we hear that there should be increased individual production.
In the course of his remarks the leader of the opposition has said that he considers that the government is primarily responsible for the inflationary situation which admittedly exists today. He went on to say that the government had not taken one single step by using measures open to it to check this inflation. Then he proceeded to enlarge at various times on what he considered to be the cure for this condition. I must confess that I am in complete agreement with a number of the suggestions that he made, but in the course of his remarks he contradicted himself so many times that I am really not just sure what he would do if he had the responsibility of directing government policy.
I am very happy to accept the suggestion of the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra and discuss what I conceive to be and what I think are generally recognized as the fundamental causes of inflation, and what are the best ways of meeting it. Before I do that, however, lest anyone may be under any misapprehension that the Minister of Finance is not just as much concerned in doing what it may be possible to do to check inflationary tendencies, let me hasten to disabuse his mind on that point. I do not want to introduce a personal note into these things but
speaking as an individual, in common with perhaps a number of others in this house, I have the greater portion of my savings in the form of life insurance, and I am just as much interested in maintaining the integrity and the stability of the Canadian dollar as any other member of the house or any other

The Address-Mr. Abbott
person in Canada. Therefore do not let anyone think that this matter is being taken lightly by myself or by the government.
As I had occasion to say at the special session last September, the root cause of any sustained inflation is an excess of spendable income as against the available supply of goods at current prices to meet it. Consequently the fundamental cure for an inflationary situation is increased production and, if necessary, draining off such excess of spending power as may exist; in other words, maximize production, minimize waste and reduce competitive expenditures such as government expenditures. I think those principles are recognized by all students of this sort of thing. That is the fundamental attack on inflation, and any other collateral remedies, such as controls, which I shall deal with a little later, are useless-they are only auxiliary-unless the fundamental fiscal and monetary policy which attacks inflation at its root is followed through and followed through vigorously.
My hon. friend said that the government had done nothing to check these inflationary forces. Before I touch on that perhaps I might say that I agree in large measure with the enumeration made by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra of the various steps which should be taken to attack inflation at its source: increased production; all fiscal and monetary measures such as reduced government expenditures; heavier taxation; budgetary surplus; increase in the interest rate; decrease of credit; reduced personal consumption; higher personal savings; reduced capital expenditures by business; direct controls; the allocation of scarce materials, and so on. With that enumeration I agree; those are various methods by which inflation can be attacked at its source.
Let me point out briefly to the house what has been done as a result of government policy since early last summer, when the admittedly strong inflationary forces which exist today first began to make themselves apparent. I said this in September, and I repeat it today. Early last spring it appeared that the strong post-war inflationary forces had run their course and that prices had pretty well levelled off. Then, of course, came Korea, and since the end of June or early July world conditions have made for the creation of strong inflationary forces not only in Canada but throughout the whole civilized world.
First, what are the fundamental cures for inflation? Increased production. A good deal can be done in that field by increasing efficiency, by getting more elderly people into the

working force, by employing more women, by all of us working a bit harder and if necessary a bit longer. As has been said before in this house, 'we are in an economy which is working pretty well at capacity. I think there is room for increased production by some of the means I have suggested; by improved efficiency, by harder work, by bringing in older groups, and so on. But the extent to which we can carry our greatly increased defence effort by increased production is limited, as I have said before. The weight of defence superimposed upon an economy already operating at a high level will mean inevitably that it must be at the expense of some of the goods and services we now enjoy as civilians. In other words the people of this country as a whole must expect a reduction in their present standard of living.
So much, then, for the effort to increase production. That is something in which the government as such can exercise little direct influence. I have used such powers of exhortation as I possess to urge all Canadians, individuals and employers and others, to endeavour to increase efficiency and production; and, Canadians being what they are, I am confident they will do so.
The second point is the use of the fiscal and monetary weapons. The hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) made a speech the other evening to which I listened with great attention and interest. He seemed to imply that we had done nothing in this field. I could not make out, any more than I could from what the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) said, just exactly what he thought the government should do, but I gathered that somehow or other we had failed to exercise some controls over the banks, as to the type of loans they should make. Let me enumerate briefly some of the things the government has done in the fiscal and monetary field. First I come to the reduction of government expenditures; and my hon. friend the leader of the opposition has strongly urged that we should effect a reduction in government expenditure on civilian account. I agree that we should effect every dollar of reduction we possibly can, because the demands of the government are competing with other demands, and consequently to the extent those demands can be cut down it helps reduce the inflationary pressure.
As soon as the added responsibilities which were to fall upon us as the result of the outbreak of the Korean war became apparent, we inaugurated a detailed review of government expenditure. I requested all departments to review their programs for the current year and postpone or eliminate any expenditures which could properly be postponed or eliminated. The house will appreciate that where

The Address-Mr. Abbott
works are under way or contracts are let, it is not easy to do that quickly; but I am happy to say we have achieved substantial results in that regard. The expenditures for the first nine months of this year, up to the end of December, are below those of last year in most departments. They are substantially below the estimates presented to and voted by this house; and I venture to say that when we close our books at the end of this fiscal year a very creditable result in the way of a reduction in controllable civilian expenditures will have been achieved. In both my budget speeches last year I made appeals to provincial and municipal governments to cut down as far as possible on their Inon-essential expenditures, and I have directed similar appeals to corporations and private individuals.
In the next place, by way of fundamental attack on the inflationary problem, we have not only been following a full pay-as-you-go policy, but today we are running a substantial surplus, which means that we are taking out of the spending stream more than we are putting back in the shape of the goods and services we are buying from the people of Canada. I never like to compare ours with other administrations, but the United States administration has been appealing for just that sort of thing. We have done it both rigorously and effectively, and in fact the budgetary surplus of Canadian federal government expenditures for the calendar year 1950 would run very close to $450 million. That surplus is still running high in these last few critical months, and that has been so for two reasons. The first is because our actual expenditures are running substantially below the estimates which were approved by this house, and in the second place because our revenues have been running substantially ahead of the revenues I estimated both last March and last September. Still we have been making very effective use of the budgetary weapon by not only fully balancing our budget but by actually attaining a substantial surplus.
In addition to that we have been making, in my judgment, full use of all practical monetary policies. As the house well knows, the Bank of Canada raised its rediscount rate last October. While the rediscount rate has perhaps ceased to have the significance it had a few years ago, interest rates have been allowed to rise; and the changes in those rates, particularly in the short-term rates, have been quite significant. But perhaps most significant of all in this use of the monetary weapon to attack the inflationary forces was the action we took last summer to offset the inflow of capital from the United States prior to releasing the exchange rate of the 80709-20
Canadian dollar. The house, of course, is aware of that huge inflow; 1 have referred to it before. The increase in our reserves in the third quarter of 1950 exceeded $536 million, and for the year as a whole amounted to the tremendous total of $625 million.

That may be, but others do not share that opinion. In the circumstances of this huge inflow of capital, which as anyone who knows anything about these things appreciates was bound to have a highly inflationary effect upon our economy unless measures were taken to offset it, we were very fortunate that we did have a large cash surplus in our government accounts which enabled us to finance an important part of that increase without recourse to borrowing.
It is true, as was pointed out by the member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell), we did have to have recourse to additional borrowing to the extent of $200 million of the $625 million. But in addition to the use of that large cash surplus, the Bank of Canada had to take, and did take, aggressive action to hold down the cash reserves of the chartered banks. A study of its weekly and monthly statements will show that during those few critical weeks to which I have referred the bank sold several hundred million dollars of government securities out of its portfolios in the open market.
In his remarks the other night the member for Greenwood (Mr. Macdonnell) seemed to me-perhaps I am doing him a bit of an injustice-to flounder around a bit in discussing the central bank's capacity to control loans by the chartered banks. I must confess that I was not sure what he had in his mind, and I do not know whether he was quite clear in his own mind. He certainly did not make it clear to me.

I do not mean to suggest that the policies which I have been outlining, budgetary policies, monetary policies, fiscal policies and so on, can operate perfectly under all conditions. For instance, with the soundest fundamental anti-inflationary policy in the world, a completely balanced budget, a full use of the interest rate, and so on, if people will not accept the inevitable consequences of the draining off of supplies as a result of the war effort, and insist on wage increases in order to compensate for the increased costs of war, or if they insist on utilizing


past savings to maintain their present level of consumption, then of course the pressure on available supplies will not, for the time being, be significantly lessened by the operation of these fiscal measures.
Some member, I forget who it was although it may have been the member from Greenwood, referred to the freeing of the Canadian dollar in September. As anyone who knows about these things will appreciate, that was, in itself, an anti-inflationary move.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My hon. friend contented himself in his speech with making assertions, and I have been outlining some positive measures which have been taken to protect it.
On the question of direct controls, one of the few positive things he said in his speech was that he was for price control. He did not say whether it was over-all price control. He carefully skated around the inevitable corollary of wage controls, but he did say he was in favour of some measure of price controls. The government has had some considerable experience in the administration of price controls, both on a selective and overall basis. If I may say so with proper modesty, I have personally had a considerable measure of experience in that field, because I pretty well lived with it from 1943 on when I was first appointed parliamentary assistant to my predecessor, Mr. Ilsley.
As my friend the member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green) pointed out the other night, we all know that controls as such do not cure anything. Under certain conditions and certain circumstances, they may be a necessary adjunct to the proper fiscal and monetary policies. This is what I said about

'that last September, alter speaking about direct controls, and this is found on page 420 of Hansard:
At best direct controls can do little more than contain for a time the pressure of demand; they do not reduce those pressures, nor do they go to the root of the matter. Their proper role is to support and buttress or, if you like, to protect the flanks of fiscal and monetary policy when we have reached the point of the practical limits of taxation.
Let me hasten to say at once, Mr. Speaker- and I am sure I am not revealing any budgetary secrets-that I do not think we have yet reached the practical limits of taxation. As I have had occasion to say in other circumstances, in a full-out war economy you come to a point where it is both administratively and practically impossible to devise a tax scheme which will raise the full amount of your war expenditures as you go along. Human nature being what it is, the effect of such an attempt is that you destroy incentive and reduce the productivity upon which the real fight against inflation depends. We have not reached that point yet.
I am now in the middle of a detailed consideration of the estimates, which I hope will be completed in the fairly near future. As has been suggested, I shall have them before the house for consideration at the earliest possible date. When that task is completed, I shall be in a position to give detailed consideration to the budgetary recommendations which I intend to put before my colleagues and the house. I will say this, and I have said it before; I intend to budget this year for a fully balanced budget, and that in itself is I think one of the fundamental attacks on this problem of inflation.
Up to the present time I think it is fair to say that a substantial degree, certainly by far the greater degree, of the inflationary price rise which we have experienced in this country has been due to forces operating abroad, either prices in countries from which we have to import such a substantial portion of our raw materials or the export prices of our products determined by the prices available in those markets. As I say, we know the value of controls. We know their limitations. We believe we know when they can be made most effective. We have taken powers to exercise selective controls and we are exercising them now. On the order paper there is a resolution, upon which a bill will be founded, asking for wider powers of control. I think it is fair to say that the government will not hesitate to recommend and to bring into force such control measures- whether they are price control measures, wage control measures or otherwise-as it
The Address

Mr. Abbott deems necessary in order to protect the Canadian economy; and it will bring them in at the time it believes they are necessary and :an be made effective.
In a consideration of this problem of inflation I think we must realize that we are heavily dependent upon forces which are completely outside our own control. I do not want to oversimplify these things. I think it is perhaps fair to say that we cannot expect to experience a much less degree of inflation in Canada than is experienced in the United States. If we do not keep our own house in order, if we do not do the things that we need to do in order to take care of our domestic problems, we can of course sustain a much greater degree of inflation. But inflation is not entirely a matter of formulas or arithmetical computations. It depends upon personal behaviour and upon psychology. In addition to the measures I have been outlining for this fundamental attack on inflation at its roots, if each individual Canadian will make up his mind that he is going to work perhaps a little bit harder and not try to get a bit of an edge on the other fellow because he is afraid that the other fellow may get an edge on him, and if we all put our backs into this task, I am not in any way pessimistic as to what the end result will be.
I believe that essentially Canadians are a common-sense people. I think common sense is one of our outstanding characteristics. I do not think that Canadians are a people who work on the principle, "I'll look out for myself and the devil take the hindmost." The government will do what it can do and what it should do to check inflationary forces. But make no mistake about it, Mr. Speaker, this is not one of the things you can cure by passing a law. Too many people believe in the philosophy: This is a bad thing; there ought to be a law against it. This is not one of those forces which can be cured by passing any law. It can be contained, having regard to our domestic economy, by following sound policies along the lines which I have been outlining. In order to be successful it will require the co-operation and the participation of the Canadian people; and I believe that that co-operation and that assistance will be forthcoming.
I do not believe that a system of over-all price or wage controls would be either desirable or effective at this time. Make no mistake about it; one cannot go into this thing for any length of time in a piecemeal manner.

speechtext: First of all, Mr. Speaker, let me say to the minister, who has outlined what he contends the government has done to protect the Canadian people from the rising cost of living, that the proof of the pudding is in the eating. Prices have continued to rise. I recall that a couple of years ago the minister, not in this house but at a press conference, said that he hoped that prices would level off- he did not say that they would; I want to be fair to him-at an index figure of somewhere, and I am speaking from memory, between 140 and 145.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I said about 145.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Yes, about 145. Last summer, at the time that the Korean war began, our cost of living index had already exceeded 165 points and at the present moment the cost of living index in this country has reached 172.5, the highest point in our history. The minister has outlined what the government has done and I say that the government's policy, if it was intended to assist the Canadian people in this period of the rising cost of living, has failed in its objective. On the other hand, during the war we find that by means of controls and subsidies the cost of living was stabilized.
We are not proposing the subamendment to this house on any doctrinaire principle. We are proposing it because we have believed and now believe that had we continued to exercise not entire control of the economy, as has been suggested, but some control of the economy in these post-war years, the cost of living in this country would not have inflicted on the Canadian people the hardship it has inflicted ever since 1945. In this house in 1946 there was a sentiment for the continuance of subsidies on certain primary necessities of life for the Canadian people. I remember how, in August of 1946 upon a motion moved by one of my colleagues in this group, this house voted for the continuance of the subsidy on milk in order to assist both the producer and the consumer. The house voted in favour of our motion. Yet within six

weeks of that vote the government discontinued that subsidy and in effect flouted the will of the elected representatives of the people. Since then step by step we have seen the removal of subsidies, the removal of controls, the rise in prices and the unprecedented heights to which rents have gone in this country.
Tonight the minister has defended what the government has done, and I am saying that the government has failed. We welcome the leader of the opposition's support for the subamendment, but again let me remind the house that when we were fighting for a continuance of intelligent controls and beneficial subsidies my hon. friends of the Progressive Conservative party joined with the government of Canada in voting against the continuance of those controls and subsidies. To the leader of the opposition and to the Progressive Conservative party may I say that my hon. friend who moved this motion (Mr. Herridge) made it perfectly clear that this was not being done from any doctrinaire standpoint so far as we were concerned. In moving this subamendment, as reported at page 156 of Hansard of February 7, he said:
For the sake of my good friends to my right and my friends immediately opposite, who are listening to me with considerable interest, I should like to make this point clear. Price controls, and the necessary subsidies, do not constitute socialism. They are an attempt, under capitalism, consciously to regulate the system so that it will work for the greater advantage of the greater number. There is nothing very frightening about that, and nothing radical about it. It is just an attempt to bring order out of chaos and to bring stability to our financial and economic system, so that the people of this country will have a cost of living that is reasonably stable, and so that we shall have a wage structure that is necessarily more' stable because of that price structure.
The leader of the opposition said that he could picture the Politburo in Moscow with a chart watching the inflation in our countries. I can picture them also, and so can a very influential and prominent Conservative in Great Britain. The fact is that is the very thing he warned about in his most recent article in Maclean's magazine. I refer of course to Mr. Beverley Baxter. Incidentally, I have not always quoted him with approval, but on this occasion I think he drives home the point that the leader of the opposition makes, and the point which is very much in my mind as I see this rising cost of living.
I say to the house now, as I have said before, that if you want to increase the support for communism in this country, or anywhere else, you make it impossible for the ordinary man to live decently. At that point you will find that communist propaganda

becomes very effective, and the best propagandists for communism are not the members of the Labour-Progressive party in this country. They are the people who today are taking advantage of the inflationary factors in our economy, who are shooting up in an unwarranted way the price structure, and who are trying to reap undue profits out of the present difficult situation in the country.
In discussing the tremendous expenditures proposed in Europe and elsewhere for rearmament Mr. Baxter says this:
There will be threatening incidents in Europe which will cause the western world to increase its mounting expenditure on rearmament and take more and more men from industry into the armed forces while, with the cunning of the Oriental and the patience of the Slav, Stalin will try to crash the western world economically through inflation caused by rearmament. Obviously, if communism is ever to become a force in the western world, the best way is to force up prices until the poor and the lowest-paid workers find life almost unendurable.
I say that I agree with that statement in Maclean's magazine made by Mr. Beverley Baxter. The government has not taken the steps to meet this situation. Indeed the very speech of the minister tonight and the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) the other night, in which they both intimated that perhaps sometime in the future controls would be put into effect, is an invitation to certain types of businessmen- and they are not all alike; please do not misunderstand me-to push prices up and take all the traffic will bear in the hope that if they get them high enough, and the price level is stabilized at that point, they will continue to reap undue profits.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation

speechtext: They will be set.

speechtext:
In other words, they will be all set. As a matter of fact, you have only to go into the stores in this city to know how prices have been pushed up over the last few weeks. On Saturday I had a letter from a man in Swift Current, and he asked me if I could explain to him why three boxes of matches, which a few weeks ago were selling at 23 cents, were that day in the store in the city where he lived 33 cents. Or can anybody explain to me why, for example, if I may speak personally as the minister did, a collar which I bought a week ago, an Arrow collar, which I could buy in New York in November for 29 cents, plus one cent tax, 30 cents in all-and I bought them there-cost me 65 cents in a local store? When I asked the reason I was told, "Oh, well you see, the price has gone up during the last two or three weeks." Clothing, particularly shirts as well as all the articles that comprise a
The Address-Mr. Coldwell child's clothes, boots and shoes and so on, are being shot up to a level so that if the prices are controlled they will be controlled at the very highest price.
I say to the Minister of Finance when he brings down his budget I hope he will not neglect to deal with this kind of thing by clapping on an excess profits tax to drain back this kind of money which has been taken out of the Canadian people. I would like to see him do something else as well. The leader of the opposition mentioned speculation. Over the last number of years we have seen people take profits out of common stocks, out of property such as housing, and so on, without turning a hand.
Years ago, during the first war, I suggested a capital gains tax. I think that one of the most fruitful sources of revenue that we could find would be a capital gains tax, a tax on unearned increment, on all sorts of things, including the stocks that the speculator deals with. He toils not, neither does he spin, but he has all the wealth of Solomon, lacking perhaps his wisdom. He has his wealth, and if I may carry the metaphor just a little further, he sometimes lives as Solomon did in other respects. I suggest a capital gains tax to catch the speculator who has been taking the cream off the economy.
Bear this in mind. We are making large governmental expenditures. I remember the tribute that was paid to the price controls system that was put into effect during the war. Let me read it. The Right Hon. J. L. Ilsley who was minister of finance during the war, in dealing with the emergency powers under which we exercised control, had this to say. When he was dealing with this bill of course he was no longer minister of finance. He was minister of justice. This is what he said, as reported at page 1926 of Hansard of April 1, 1947:
It is estimated that government expenditures averaged $4 billion a year between 1942 and 1946. Without price control this cost might have been at the very least twenty-five per cent higher. I think that twenty-five per cent is based upon the other figures which I have given with regard to the additional percentage which the consumers would have been obliged to pay; and the stabilization program has thus meant a saving of another billion dollars a year. From these estimates it is possible to see that the cost of the control program was under $200 million a year, while the savings to the consumer purchasers and government as a buyer were on this hypothesis possibly $2J billion a year. The figures are tentative but do give some idea of the relative magnitude of the cost of and the savings effected by the government price control program.
If you divide $2J billion by $200 million which it cost, you find that for every dollar we spent on these controls we saved for the

The Address-Mr. Coldwell consumers and the country, and after all consumers also make up the population of the country, $12.50.
The argument was made, of course, that we could not do this kind of thing in peacetime. Very well; we thought that we could. But in any event we are now in what is virtually a war economy, or so close to a war economy, that it is very difficult to make any distinction between this economy and a wartime economy.
When the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Claxton) comes before the house and tells us we are going to spend $1,600 million on defence preparation in the next year, and that we are going to spend $5 billion in the next three years, then we are embarking upon a spending program on behalf of the people of Canada, apart altogether from the people of the country as individuals, which does approach the wartime economy when controls and subsidies proved to be so beneficial. When I say "approached" I am not pretending that they are expenditures right up to wartime; but aft least they are approaching wartime figures.
The minister shakes his head. What are peacetime budgets? Well, I was here before the war. I was here before we had wartime budgets and post-war budgets. I remember that in the pre-war years we thought a budget of $550 million for this country was a very substantial one. I can remember how in June of 1939, when my hon. friends of the Social Credit party wanted to move for an issue of $200 million worth of currency by the Bank of Canada, it was opposed. At that time I suggested a compromise, that we ask for $100 million which, to me, seemed reasonable. We were told by the then minister of finance, the Hon. Charles Dunning, that we nad accepted a budget of over $500 million: Where did we think we could get another $100 million? Those were peacetime budgets. Budgets we have had since the outbreak of the second world war were either wartime budgets or post-war budgets made necessary because of the conditions arising out of the war. They were wartime budgets in that sense. And when we see that this year we are going to spend an additional billion dollars and more on defence over what we have been used to spending in the last few years, one can see that this is bound to have an inflationary effect, unless we exercise some measures of control.
I agree with the minister that an answer, of course, is increased productivity. He said tonight that we had no pool of unemployed in the sense that we had a pool of unemployed in 1939, that we have no idle machines, that


every available resource we can produce is being utilized by industry in one way or another.
Of course I believe we could improve our productivity to some extent by improving our industrial organization, by improving our machinery and so on. But I think all we could do in that respect would not be sufficient to increase production to the extent that would be necessary to keep down the present inflation.
So we have to do something else. We suggest that other measures should be taken. The leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew) is quite right; we give these two, price controls and subsidies, as two of the things which should be done. And, incidentally, we believe that they should be done. May I add that when I mention price controls I am also thinking of rent controls. I do not in my own mind differentiate between one sort of price and another sort of price, the prices of commodities and the price paid for a place in which a man and his family shall live.

speechtext: What about wages?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Someone says, "What about wages?" I will not dodge that question. We have today a very substantial measure of wage controls. We have a substantial measure of the control of farm prices. The farmer who produces wheat in the prairie provinces today in large part-not wholly- is controlled by the world wheat agreement. As the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) knows well, organizations with which he is connected make agreements for a year in advance. Some wage agreements are for two years in advance, and those wages are controlled.
Let me add immediately that if we have the proper kind of controls in effect in this country-price, rent and other controls- and the leaders of the unions and workers are brought into conference, I am convinced agreements can be worked out that would stabilize wages. That could be done, if prices were controlled. Because, remember, wages have been chasing prices-not prices chasing wages, as is so often said.
So that today we are in an economy which is virtually, in the sense in which 1 now use the term, a wartime economy. Higher productivity-yes. But higher productivity will not meet the needs of the current situation. So I say that in my opinion the government should not wait until clothing, furniture and a hundred and one other commodities which enter into the daily living of the people of Canada have been pushed up to the top level, and then stabilize the

price level. I think attempts should be made, indeed, to roll back those prices, so that many people in this country could have some hope.
I understood what the leader of the opposition said when he spoke about the depreciation of the Canadian dollar. I do not think he said what the Minister of Finance interpreted him as saying. What he said was an actual fact, of course, that the dollars of the people invested in insurance, victory bonds and other savings, would buy when the investment was made almost twice as much as they will buy today. To that extent the purchasing power of a dollar in a bond has certainly depreciated.
I think it is the duty of the government to see to it that those savings of the people are protected, and that there is also protection for the standard of living of those who have
The Address-Mr. Coldwell suffered, those who are living on savings and pensions-old age and veterans, industrial and otherwise. In our opinion that can be done only by doing far more than the government has already done. Some of the things that should be done are the putting into effect immediately of price controls and the paying of subsidies to primary producers so that consumer goods will cost less; and that a real attempt should be made to roll back prices and to organize our economy so that we shall have some economic stability and essential unity among our people in the great national effort we are being called upon to undertake.
